ring's Clugh ----- ROBE= OP LINCOLN. on brier and weed, el'irrelarlYtsheitnegsitngof his little dame, Over the mountain-side or mead, Robert of Lincoln is telling his nante Bob-o'-link, bob-o'-link, Spink, spank, spink ; snug and safe is that nest of ours, Bidden among the summer flowers. Chee, chee. chee. Robert of Lincoln is gaily drest, Wearing a bright black wedding coat; White are his shoulders, and white his crest. Hear him call in his merry note : Bob-o'-link, bob-o'-link. Spink, spank, spink ; Look, what a nice new coat is mine., Sure there never was a bird so fine, Chee, chee, chee. 'Robert of Lincoln's Quaker wife. Pretty and quiet, with plain brown wings, sl.„l.assing at home a patient life, • •” Broods in the grass while her husband singe; , Bob-or-link, bob-o'-link, Spink, spank, spink ; Brood, kind creature; you need not fear Thieves and robbers while I am here Chee, chee. chee.

modest and shy as a nun is she, One weak chirp is her only note; Braggart and prince of braggarts is he, Pouring boasts from his little throat Bob-o'-link, bob-o'-link, Spink, spank, spink ; Never was I afraid of man; Catch me, cowardly knaves, if you can; Chee, chee, chee. Six white eggs, on a bed of hay, Flecked with purple, a pretty sight! There, as the mother sits all day, Robert is singing with all his might Bob-o'-link, Spink, spank, spink ; Nice good wife, that never goes out. Keeping house while I frolic about; Chee, chee, chee. Soon as the little ones chip the shell, Six wide mouths are open for food; Robert of Lincoln bestirs him well, Gathering seeds for the hungry brood. Bob-o'-link, Spink, spank, spink. This new life is likely to be Hard for a gay young fellow like me; Chee, chee, chee.

Robert of Lincoln at length is made Sober with work, and silent with care Off is his holiday-garment laid, Ralf forgotten that merry air : Bob-o'-link, bob-o'ink, Spink, spank, spink, Nobody knows, but my mate and I, Where our nest and our nestlings lie; Oboe, chee, chee. Summer wanes; the children are grown. Fun and frolic no more he knows; Robert of Lincoln's a humdrum crone Off he files, and we sing as he goes Bob-o'-link, bob-o'-link, Spink, spank, spink ; Whea you can pipe that merry old strain, Robe t of Lincoln, come back again; Chee, chee, chee.

THE LATE SIR CHARLES REED AND MR. PEABODY.— From his childhood Charles Reed was filled with a desire to be useful. The writer of this sketch spent some years with him at school, and for some time in the same class, and ' looking back on those distant days feels how true it was in his case that the child is the father of the man. The bright and sunny spirit, the genial and equable temper, and con- stant activity which were characteristic of his riper years, were with him as a boy. He was marked out for a course of active philanthropy, and even in those days was ready to interest himself in the work of the Sunday school or in other services of a like kind. PARODY ON " THE CATARACT OF LODORE."—" ROW THE DACCHTERS COME DOWN AT DIINOON." How do the daughters Come down at Dunoon ? Daintily, Tenderly, Gingerly, Glidingly, Blidingly, Blippingly, ' Skippingly, Trippingly, Chippingly, Bumpingly, Thumpingly, Clumpingly- Starting and bolting, And darting and jolting. And tottering and staggering, And lumbering and slithering. And hurrying and scurrying, And worrying and flurrying, And rushing and leaping and crushing and creeping, Feathers a-flying all—bonnets untying all— Petticoats rapping and flapping and slapping all. Crinolines flowing and blowing And showing all. Balmorals, dancing and glancing, entrancing all; Feats of activity— Nymphs on declivity— Mothers in eestacies— Fathers in vextacies— Lady-loves whisking and frisking and clinging on. True-lovers puffing and blowing and springing on. Dashing and clashing and shying and flying on. Blushing and flushing and wriggling and giggling on, Teasing and pleasing and squeezing and wheezing on. Everlastingly falling and bawling and sprawling on, Tumbling and rumbling and grumbling and stumbling on Any fine afternoon, About July or June— That's just bow the daughters Come down at Dunoon —Mr. C. Pennell.

SYSTEM 1 .F LAND TEN LIRE. At the suggestion of Mr. Gladstone the Cobden Club has, through Cassell, Petter, Galpin, and Company, issued a new edition of "Systems of Land Tenure in various Countries." The Premier no doubt feels that the public needs a good deal of reliable information regarding the agrarian laws of our own and other countries, not only in view of the great measure now before the constituencies relating to Ireland, but preliminary to the consideration of the land law reform which must before long be applied to England as well. The essays comprised in this v, lurne cannot but be of great ser- vice in supplying such valuable data, and should be care- fully read by all who desire to understand intelligently the various points involved in a discussion of the many-sided land question. Mr. J. W. Probyn, the editor, in his preface, which points out hbw gladly the committee of the Cobden Club have complied with Mr. Gladstone's suggestion, ex- plains that ill-health has prevented Mr. Cliffe Leslie from bringing up the facts contained in his essay on the French system to the present time, though substantially it remains a fair description, but in arrear of the statistics now obtain- able. The original essays of the Right Hon. M. Longfield (Ireland), Sir George Campbell (India), and the Hon. George Brodrick (Primogeniture) have, he remarks, been carefully revised, and have had additions made to them by their respective authors ; and Mr. R. B. Morier, C.B.'s " Agrarian Legislation of Prussia" has been supplemented by the publication of his report on the Tenure of Land in the Grand Duchy of Hesse, sent to the Foreign Office in 1870. Three original contributors to the series:—Mr. Wren Hoskyns (England 1, Dr. Julius Faucher (Russian Agrarian Legislation of 1871), and Mr. C. M. Fisher (Farm and Land laws of the United States) are dead and their essays have therefore bees published just as they were written. The only essay remaining to be mentioned is that on the land system of Belgium and Holland. This is by the cele- brated economist, M. Emile de Laveleye. We cannot of course hope in the limited space here at our disposal to even summarise the leading points emphasised in the book by these eminent authorities who furnish in the aggregate a body of evidence perfectly unique in its completeness. Beyond a slight reference to Judge Longfield's contribution to the theme we propose only to draw special attention to Mr. Brodrick's chapters on the law and custom of Primo- geniture. These we select because in them the writer gives for the purposes of his argument, a summary of foreign land laws which elsewhere in the volume are treated in detail. First, then, a few words concerning the exhaustive essay which occupies the place of honour, "The tenure of land in Ireland." The writer was formerly Judge of the Landed Estates Court in Ireland. He handles his subject with the skill and the familiarity which could only follow from a deep practical knowledge of the difficulties to be overcome in farming laws that shall do justice alike to the two classes chiefly concerned—the landlords and the tenants. The Judge does not touch on some of the plans which are put forward for dealing with Irish discontent in respect of the land laws, but addresses himself with great detail to acknowledged grievances, and indicates what seem to he thoroughly practical proposals for their removal. As already pointed out in the leading columns of The Guardian several of Judge Longfield's suggested alterations in the law are embodied in the Governm nt measure which Mr. Gladstone last week introduced into Parliament. In his concise account of primogeniture in England Mr. Brodrick takes cognisance, as we have said, of the land :sys- tems inherited or adopted by other civilised nations. tern of land occupation may be generally small proprietors. The conclusion (sums up Mr. Brodrick) to be drawn from a comprehensive review of foreign land systems may be expressed In a few sentences. No other nation has adopted in its en- tirety the English right of Primogeniture—a right which could only have grown up in a thoroughly feudalised society, and which could only have been perpetuated in a country where the feudal structure of society has never undergone any vio- lent disturbance. In those States which have remodelled their jurisprudence on the principles of the Code Napoleon, the eldest son is effectually debarred from engrossing the whole landed property of the family. Iwother States which have developed their law of succession independently parents are allowed to make eldest sons under greater or less restrictions. In no considerable State but our own does the law itself, in de- fault of a will'or settlement, constitute the eldest son the sole heir to all the realty, and in no other is the exclusive prefer- ence to the first born thus consecrated by law carried to such extreme lengths in family government. No highly civilised people but the English tolerate the dominion of a bygone generation over the greater part of the national soil under settlements and entails designed to limit the ownership and control the action of living owners. In no other part of Europe, nor in the 'United States of America, nor in the British Colonies is the division of landed property so unequal, or the predominance of a landed aristocracy so firmly rooted. In no other is the free transfer of land or the power of mortgaging obtatructed by so many legal impediments, by so great a risk of delay,or by the certainty of so exorbitant a cost. Nowhere else is the land habitually occupied by a class of tenants who hold only from year to year, and cultivated by a class of labourers divorced from the soil and working for weekly wages. Dealing with the fallacies which beset the social argu- ment in favour of Primogeniture, our essayist ridicules the contention that entails and settlements are effectual in giving a resident proprietary. He points out that most of our great aristocratic heuses possess more than one family place, that it is impossible for the head of the family to re- side at each, and that, in short, absenteeism is the inevitable consequence. The more thoroughly (it is argued finally) we appreciate the almost insuperable difficulty of partially reforming an institu- tion so deeply rooted and widely ramified as the custom of entail and settlement, the more irresistible will appear the conclusion that it is better to reform it altogether, by abolish- ing all kinds of ownership, except ownership in fee simple, with all customary and copyhold tenures, and by imposing proper restrictions on the length of leases. The conception of such a measure would demand an effort of constructive statesmanship quite as bold as that of an Irish Land Bill, while Its execution would affect still vaster interests, and must be spread over a longer period of time. Once carried, however, it would cut half the knots which together make up the English Land Question. It is noteworthy that in the essay on Irish Land Tenure utterance is given by Judge Longfield to sentiments iden- tical with those just quoted, the statement being that nothing would tend more to the creation of yeomen aid peasant proprietors than the abolition of the law of Primo- geniture and of settlement. Like testimony is borne by the late Mr. C. Wren Hoskyns in the essay on the Land Laws of England. Indeed, the main purpose in publishing the essays is the enforcement of this doctrine of freeing the land. How far the writers have succeeded we must now leave intending readers to judge. * Systems of Land Tenure in Various Countries : Cassell, Fetter, Gal pin and Co., London, Paris, and New York.

DEPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—Mownay. FUGITIYF OFFENDERS BILL.—The LORD Cnawcarzow introduced a Bill to amend the law as to fugitive offenders, which was read a first time. TEE Tamil JURY ',mos.—The Marquis of LANSDOWNE moved for a committee to inquire into the operation of the Irish jury laws as regards trial by jurrin criminal cases.— Lord CARLINGFOI2D, speaking for the Government, thought a very promised that the , Government would render all the good ease had been made out for inquiry, and assistance in their power. The motion was then agreed to.

• HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Moroar. Pmnac Busieless.—Replying to Mr. Thomasson, Mt.-, GLADSTONE declared, amidst loud cheers, that the condition of the House with regard to the arrangements for the tran- saction of public business constituted a public question of the first magnitude, and promised that it should receive the earliest attention of the Government. .Tlre RANT To GENERAL Ronntrrs.—There were two questions on the paper relating to the proposal to make a present of £12,000 to Sir F. Roberts for his services in " Afghanistan. One of these, by Lord R. Churchill, embodied a silly rumour to the effect that Sir F Roberts was pro- mitied £25,000, and that the amount was afterwards reduced to £12,090.—Lord Hawrieterrow, in explaining that this suggeettola Was entirely untrue, indignantly rebuked 'Lord Randolph Churchill for putting such questions upon no other grounds than those contained "in the caluminous and lying gossip which appeared in certain newspapers that were Published in the metropolis." The fact was that upon being offered a baronetcy with a pension of £l,OOO a year, Sir Frederick Roberts felt some natural hesitation about accepting a hereditary honour when the pension attached to it was limited to one life. It was ultimately arranged that ' the general should receive the capital sum of £12,500 in lieu of a pension. PRISONERS UNDER Tire COERCION Acy.—Mr. FoRsyER informal Mr. Parnell that the confidential circular issued by the Inspector Getters; of Irish Constabulary was issued with the ligowledge anffeionsent of the Executive Government of Ireland,and of himself. _ WITUDRAWAL Dllk :47TE Plumes!. To LICENSE RAILWAY , Catts--_-Mr.GLADErrOila referring to the proposal to license railwaVearkand the opposition it had met with, said he re- garded it ai effectually killed by the menaces to which it bad been subjected. LOCAL TAXATION.—A motion by Mr.PELL, in favour of an annual Ministerial statement on the subject of local taxis- '.on and finance, led to an interesting debate, in which Sir Massey Lopes, Mr. Rathbone, and Mr. Gladstone took part.' —Sir M. LOPES illustrated the magnitude of the subject by Sating that local iridebtedness was increasing at the rate of, $10,609,09.9,;',' per " annum, and stood in round numbers at £150,000,000 a sum considerably above the rateable value of the United King- dom at the present moment.—Mr. GLADSToNE edmitted the urgent importance of the sub- ject ; again referred to the pressing question of thearrears of pubic business ; promised that the President of the Local Government Board would make a statement en local expen- diture; and suggested that it would be advisable to estab- lish is committee of weight and authority, whicn should have for its duty the regular review of local expenditure and accounts. The motion was negatived without a ,livieion. RECIFROCITir.—Mr. MaclvErt brought forward his reci- procity resolution. In' a most extraordinary speech Mr. Maciver spoke of Mr. Bright as "an individual with grey hairs," and described himself as a disciple of Mr. Ecroyd, whose absence he much deplored.—After soma remarks from Mr. Slaeg, Mr. asansvoNx appealed to hon. members to proceed with the business which awaited them.—The House afterwards went into committee, and Mr. Gladstone's budget proposals were discussed.

TILE IRISH POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.— Mr. °Toxemia. resumed the debate on the conduct of the Irish Executive, based on Mr. McCartby's motion, and in an acrid speech, discussed the conduct of the Executive. When he , I resumed his seat Mr. Litton and another member rose from , the Liberal benches. Met by loud cries from the Parnellites I for Mr. Foster, these two gentlemen resumed their seats. Mr. Forster making no sign, Mr. Litton rose again and addressed the HOUSE in support of the policy of the Govern- ment. —Mr. FORSTER, when he followed, explained his hesitation to interpose on the ground that he desired to have some arguments to answer rather than to appear in reply to personal attacks. The right hon. gentleman, turning first to the case of Father Sheehy, showed by many quotations from public reports, how the rev, gentleman had syste- matically incited the people to lawlessness, whilst declaring that if they arrested him "a chord would be touched in the Iriali heart which had not yet vibrated." The Government, Mr. Forster said, had considered the responsibility of striking such a chord, and had decided upon arresting Father Sheehy. Referring to the circular, to which his attention was noisily invited by the Irish members, Mr. Forster stated that it was issued by his authority, and he accepted the responsibility of every word of it. With respect to the policy of the Government in the future, he declared, amid loud cheers from the Ministerialists, that the Govern- ment, although not assisted by members opposite, were determined to maintain the law and to make it respected. There was a combination to make robbery successful by armed resistance. The Governmen,l wiuld do their best to meet this, first by arresting the actual perpetrators, and then by proceeding against the inciters, whether they were metn- hers .of Parliament or clergymen. He trusted that the House would by a decided vote express their confidence in the Government. For himself, all he asked for was fair play, which he was bound to say he had not received from certain sections of the House. This speech, which was delivered with much warmth, and was occasionally loudly cheered from the Ministerial benches, was marked by many interruptions from the Irish members. Mr. T. P. O'Connor, who, next to Mr. Healy, was foremost in this mode of argument, was at length gravely warned by the Speaker that if such conduct were continued it would be regarded as d;sregarding the authority of the chair. After this Mr. O'Connor subsided. Mr Healy, by more skilful observance of Parliamentary forms, was able up to the end to indulge in irritating interruptions. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. PETMONS.—Petitions were presented praying for certain amendments in the Rivers Conservancy Bill, by Lord Sandon, from the Liverpool Land and House Owners' Aseosi ciation; against the sale of intoxicating liquors in railway., carriages, by Mr. Summers, from the inhabitants of East; and Mid-Cheshire; for the repeal of the Vaccination Actg.,' by Mr. Agnew, from public meetings at Failsworth. ar TUESDAY'S COUNT OUT.—Mr. CHILDERS moved that the Committees of the House should not sit till two o'clock to- day, it being Ascension Day, and have leave to sit till sir, o'clock, notwithstanding the sitting of the Hamel' —Mr. ARTHUR ARNOLD and other hon. members complained' that the Government had not prevented the count out olle Tuesday night.—Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT said he thought private members themselves should make and keep a House on private members' nights. The labours of Parliament , were getting greater and greater, and he found them almost ' intolerable. Work began at nine in the morning, and 'ended at two the next morning; so that, as near as possible, 17 out of the 24 hours were taken up. He ventured to say, that the House would not allow such hours of labour for , any other class of Her Majesty's subjects, but would very anon bring in a bill something like the Factory Act.—Mr. Childer's motion was carried by 58 against 41 votes.— Mr. Diu..wrx moved the second reading of the bill for amending the lunacy laws; and the debate which followed will produce an uncomfortable impression, inasmuch as it was virtually admitted km all sid-ts tbat cases of improper detention in private asylums are possible, and are indeed happening, under the present inefficient system of detention. Mr. Dillwyn declared that in many instances the cure of merely excitable persons was retarded by their being com- pelled to herd with hopeless idiots and raving maniacs; and mentioned the case of a gentleman of high position and large property, who sat and voted during the last two years of the late Parliament, and who to now discharging all the duties of a landowner in Scotland. Mr. Dillwyn declared that if it had not been for his own and the Speaker's intervention, this _ ,gentleman, some of whose relatives had an interest in keep- ing him incarcerated, would still have been confined in the 'asyldm.—Mr. COURTNEY expressed entire sympathy with ' the member for Swansea in seeking the suppression of private asylums, but pointed out the inadequacy of the present bill —Sir R. Cams also strongly urged the necessity for legisla- tion, and said as a visitor to asylums he had frequently been obliged to interfere to procure the discharge of patients who were actually cured.—Sir WILLIAM HA.RCOURT afterwards intimated that he should not oppose the progress of Mr. Dillwyn's measure, and the bill was read a second time. auscimaaarEnns. The Removal Terms (Scotland) Bill was read a second time, and the Newspapers Bill passed through committee. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Thunsner. GUNS AND PISTOLS FOR IRISH LANDLORDS. Mr. MACIVER wished to know if ssveral orders for guns and pistols for Ireland had been placed at Birmingham during the last month or two; and if orders for old military Snider- Enfields had not been very plentiful lately.—Mr. CHAMIJER- LAIN replied that in the time of the late Government 200,000 Enfield rifles had been sold at about is. 6d. each, but the late Government contended that they were unserviceable and some of them dangerous. Under the present Government no such sale had taken place. Colonel Stanley interposed with the assurance that the sale of arms was stopped by the late Government, and that no sales had taken place of late years. • MR. BRADLAUGH'S SYMFATHISERS.—The HOME SECRE- TARY, on being questioned by Mr. Labouehere respecting the conduct of the police in removing certain sympathisers with Mr. Bradlaugh from the recent meeting in Exeter Hall, ex- pressed an opinion that they had performed a difficult duty with moderation and good temper. MR. SUTER'S Raxsoat.—Sir C. Daum informed the House that in order to secure the role tee of Mr. Suter, who had been captured by brigands, it bad been found necessary to pay the whole ransom demanded, but he was not aware that the security of the brigands had in any way been guaranteed. IRISH AFFAIRS.—In the course of a reply to questions on Irish affairs, Mr. GLADSTONE stated that he feared a con- siderable number of tenants able to nay rent were, under the influence of sinister suggestions, refusing pay- ment, but it was difficult to say whether it was desirable to take any fresh steps with regard to the recovery of rent. CI7STOMS AND INLAND REVFNUE SILL.—The considera- tion of the clauses of the Customs and Inland Revenue Bill was resumed in Committee, and the Bill as amended was ordered to be reported to the House. THE bum LAND BILL.—On the order of the day for Committee on the /ash Land Bill Sir W. BeurrisaoT moved that no bill would be satisfactory unless it included provi- sions enabling the court to hear all claims by landowners for compenaatien for losses proved to have been sustained under the provisions of the bill, and to award reasonable compensation. The amendment was opposed by the ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND, who refused IO admit that the latdlords were entitled to compensation.—Mr. C. E. Evan., THE TFINFT OF A HAMM, c$C., AT TARN:a{ 'RACE- COUBSE.—George Watson, John O'Neil, John aturnhv, James Evans, and Mary Evans, alias Costello, were Lain brought up on remand charged with having, at Taf,,,k racecourse, on Saturday, the 23rd April, stolen a hemp, containing knives and forks, silver cups and spoons, bottles of champagne and 'claret, towels, &c., the property of Mr. John Piggott, of Grassendale Park, Oarston, near Liver- pool.—The police stated that the principal witness was at present in prison, and the prisoners were again remanded till next Wednesday, when the case will be fully gone into and disposed of. THEFT OF A PAIR OF CLOS.—Margaret Travis was charged with stealing a pair of clogs, value 25., from the dwelling-house of John Woodward. Holmes' Buildings, St. Helens-road, Eccleston, sometime between the 9th and 1611 instant.—P.C. Prior deposed that he apprehended the prisoner on the previous Sunday morning. He charged her with stealing the clogs in question, and she replied, "Well, I took the clogs from the door, and 1 intend to put them back again."—James Henry Potter, assistant to Mr. Morton, pPlaewdngbedrotkieier,ciko:gc:lpersodtonu-cseVdeaett,h his ihdopthoe p n threisioontehr instant, and be lent her 9d. on thern.—Jane Weave, wife of Francis Gleare, No- 10, Rowson-street, add that on Sunday, the 15th instant, prisoner asked her to purchase a pawn- ticket for a pair of clogs from her for 6d. Iler son bought the ticket and took out the clogs from the pawnshop. The Clogs produced were the same.—Prisoner, who had nothing to say, was remanded till the following day, when she was was brought np at the Widnes Petty Sesions and sentenced to one rormatb'e ilnpisonme,t.

That was a circumstance which, he thought, showed that he did not neglect his •familv.—The complainant said the defendant , offered to give her £5O if she would leave him, and had i brought a paper with him for her to 'sign. She had, how- ' ever, resolutely refused to sign any paper.—Alderman Chandley said there was just one step between what defen- dant had been guilty of and absolute murder, and it was very evident to him the defendant and his wife could never hope to be happy together. The defendant would be fined £lO and costs for the assault upon his wife, and the Bench would make an order for a legal separation, the defendant to pay £1 per week for the maintenance of his wife and two cbildren.—The defendant: I am not in a position to do it, sir. A JuverviLe Tatum—Ralph Norman, a boy 11 years of age, was charged with stealing, en the 20th May, a silver Geneva watch, of the value of 158., the property of Emma Kay, of No. 17, Orford-street. —On Friday morning, the prisoner was sent to the prosecutrix's house with a message, and after he had gone the watch Mrs. Kay had left on the mantleshelf was missed. The same day, a Mr. Hackles called at the police station, bringing with him a watch, I which the prisoner had sold to his son for a few " stonies" or ' marbles. The prisoner was then searched for by the police, and afterwards taken into custody—The Bench addressed a few words of caution to the prisoner, and sentenced him to receive six strokes with the birch rod. MONDAY.—Before His Worship the Mayor (Alderman Pick- mere), Mr. Henry Bleckly, Alderman Davies, Captain Litton, Councillors Monks and Crosfield. PITCH AND Toss.—Richard Thomas Stockton, a toy, was charged with playing at pitch and toss, in Gas-street, about six o'clock, on Saturday.—Defendant was caught in the act by P.C. Monagban.—He was ordered to pay costs. ALLEGED THEFT.—James Carrot, labourer, was charged with being drank in the Fox publichouse, on Saturday night, and also with stealing two shillings, the property of Patrick Dagnall.—Prosecutor went into the inn and pur- chased some liquor, putting down half-a-crown. Prisoner was standing near, and the servant placed the change, a 1 florin, on the table just opposite. The servant observed pri- soner take up the money and walk out, accompanied with a I woman. She then told Dagnall that a man had taken his 'change, and prisoner was followed. He was caught in the 'street, but denied the theft. Prisoner had half-a•orown, a sixpenny piece, and 5d in copper upon him when appre- hended.—Mary Giblin deposed to placing the florin on the table and prisoner taking it up, but another witness was called who stated that the servaet had placed the florin into 1 the prisoner's hand.—P.C. Hitchmough apprehended the prisoner on Saturday night, and he was then drunk. On tbat account be did not charge him with the theft until that morning. In reply to the charge prisoner said he had stolen I no monev.—For being drunk prisoner was fined ss. and I costs, and the charge of theft was dismissed. 1 Tnerr BY A. CAB DRIVER. James Davenport, cab I I driver, was charged with stealing a whip, the property of Richard Dasmett, from the premises of Mr. Connor, cab proprietor, King-street, Warrington. On Tuesday prosecu- tor took his cab into the yard, and left his whip upon it. About two hours afterwards the whip had gone, and it was ascertained that the prisoner had taken it.—Mr. Hunt said the prisoner was very ill when brought to the police station, on Saturday night, and be admitted him to bail. He had reason to believe that the illness was brought about by anxiety regarding the theft.—Prisoner expressed his con- trition for the offence, and the Bench diarnissed the charge in consequence of prisoner's state of health. A SAD CASE.—Wm. /Miley, /5 years of age, and who walked with the help of a crutch, was charged with being drunk in Dial-street, on Sunday night.—P.S. Spinka said he was passing along Dial-street at 10-45 on the previous night -when he found a mowd collected rouod the prisoner, who .Was drunk. He had a cut on the eye, and his face was very 'bloody. He (witness) thought at first the boy was dead, but after some time he got him round, and tried to obtain lodgings for him, hut failed to do so, and he was obliged to carry him to the police station.—Prisoner said he got some I beer in the Rose beerhouse.—The mayor: Who was with [ you? Prisoner: Some black militia. (Laughter.)—P.S. k Spinks said a militiaman was with the boy, who said he had .been to the barrack., and he had given him a glass of beer. --Councillor Crostielcl : It is a great -shame that people should give that boy drink. (To prisoner.) It is a terrible thieg to see a boy like you in this court.—The father of the prisoner said the boy had had no money given to him, and could not have bought the liquor.—The prisoner said he was very sorry, and he was discharged. Onscvsx LANGUAGE.—Joseph Lightfoot, a stallkolder, was summoned for using obscene language, on the sth inst., in the Market-place.— Ile was fined ss. and costs. A RUNAWAY APPRENTICE.—Luke Lowe, an apprentice, was summoned by Mr. George Artisestall, for unlawfully absenting himself from his employment, whereby a loss of £1 21. 6d. had been sustained, and which was now claimed. —He was ordered to, repay the money at the rate of is. 6d. per week, and return to his work. - SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—James Lingard was charged with neglecting to send his son to school. Fined Sc. and costs.—John Gleare was charged with not sending his daughter Martha Jane to school. Defendant's daughter ap- peared to answer the charge. Mr. Riley said the circum- stances in tide else were somewhat extraordinary. Defen- dam left his wife several years ago in consequence of 'quarrels, and he had since been living in lodgings. About three years ago defend int's wife married again at Sankey, and she was at present living at Bank Quay. The daughter who appeared that morning., and who was married, took the child Martha Jane to live with her, and the father promised ect pay her something every week, but had not rI me so. IDefendint and two eons were working for Mr. Cartwright, and earning good wages. Defendant's daughter said the t girl had lived with her for five years. She took her to nurse ' her children. Mr. Riley said the girl had only attended school 17 times in Sim years. Defendant's daughter said her father had told her he would pay the fine. Defendant was fined 58.—A fine of Si. was imposed on William Higham, for not sending his son James regularly to school. He had been about 75 times out of 116, and, though nine 'years of age, could not read or write.—A similar penalty was inflicted upon Martha Peacock, for the irregular atten- dance at school of her son Benjamin. Tattpsnay.--Bef tre Councillor Milner. 1 THE GRANTING OF RELIEF.—CURIOI7S CASE.—John I Quinn, brickmaker, was charged under a warrant with neglecting his wife and family.—Mr. Harbourne, relieving ofßeer, said that on the previous day the prisoner's wife ap- plied to the Guardians for relief for herself and two children, stating that she was destitute. Her husband was earning, she said, .£2 per week at Mr. Holmes's brickyard, but she had received nothing from him for a week, and she was without food. The Guardians decided to allow her 71 6d. per week, and ss. had been paid to her. Mr. Herbourne handed in a nete from Mr. Holmes showing prisoner's earn- ings, and it appeared that he had drawn his wife's wages also, the weekly income being about 3f/ft.—Prisoner stated be had given his wife 335. on the 14th inst., and that beshad expended his last week's wages for the benefit of his family. In support of his statement he prodnced a number of pawn tickets showing that he had spent 225. in articles of clothing and been obliged to again pawn them to buy food for him- self and son during the present week. He was quite willing to keep his family, but his wife would net keep his home.— Mr. Hunt said prisoner's wife had only a few weeks ago been released from gaol, where she bad been imprisoned seven days for stealing a pair of boots.—As prisoner's story had the appearance of truth, the magistrate wished the matter to be inquired into, and P.S. Berry went to investigate it at 'Once. On his return he said prisoner's statement was true —Prisoner expressed his willingness to repay the Guardians what they had expended if allowed time, and Mr. Han-bourne said the Guardians, considering the different complexion put upon the case, would be quite willing to grant that.—The case was therefore adjourned for a fortnight. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Alderman - Webster. . I PEACE wed Quirroess.—William Caskey, of Latchford, was charged with using threatening language towards his wife, who was afraid he would do her some bodily harm. Mrs. Caskey said she wanted peace and quietness, but would not give evidence against her husband. Prisoner was ordered to pay costs, 6s.—Catherine Robinson was charged with using language calculated to provoke a breach of the peace to Ann Melior. Mr. Moore defended, and the Cave was dismissed. Fairclongh and Sons —Mr. White said the boy did not come within the graep of ,Tie law. He was toa youne.r.—Mr.Fairelnugh stated them -vere abut 10 boys on the field on Sunday, and when he went

- —chive never seen Lord Hartiugton so angry as he was on Monday night, when denying that he had first promised Sir Frederick Roberts moo°, and then, for reasons not avowed, docked him of 167,500. The suggestion of Lord Randolph Churchill,. underlying his question' was, of course, that Sir Frederick had been punished for having an independent mind of his own on such subjects as the Afghan annexation and short service. Sir Frederick him- self certainly shares the belief that be has been made to inffer for his politics. The information came from those -who are about him, and the statement had been made in his to_resence without eliciting a denial. But it made Lord Hartington thoroughly angry, and part company with that air Of indifference and of insouciance which be usually wears. He was stirred to emphasis again when it was sug- gested that Mr. Brett, his private secretary, had been indis- creet—a charge which nobody who knows Mr. Brett would for one instant believe. The truth seems to be that Sir Frederick Robert§ asked for more than the Government decided to grant him; that he was not at once told that it. was impossible; and that, in consequence, he formed hope!' that were doomed to disappointment. Notwithstanding the printed announcement appended each copy of the New Testament, "all rights reserved," the New York Herald has printed the whole book in its pages: Of course, the paper id' outside of the copyright laws, but that fact does not lessen the indignation felt by thel' Universities of Oxford and Cambridge. Several chesP' editions have also been produced, and are being sola for fivd and ten cents the copy. The volume has also been addet to the railway bookstalls here, and is being offered Bide by, side with the daily papers, sensation novels, and cheap comic literature. Several of the popular Sunday papers to:. 14y in reviewing the new version denounce the alterations made in the Lord's Prayer. The sale, notwithstanding the unfavourable comments, continues very brisk, and the. pecuniary gain for the work promises to be enormous. Orders have already been received in this country for two million copies. The Chicago Tines had all the material corrections telegraphed from England, these running to 3,000 words. Mr. Toole has made a new departure in the class of entertainment produced at his theatre, the Folly. Last night he produced a musical extravaganza from the facile pen of Mr. R. Reece called "Welsh Rabbits." Mr. Toole is of course the central figure, and his adventures are worthy of Don Juan's travels. He falls Weep under an umbrella upon the Bands of Margate, and, like Uncle Dick, dreams a I dream in which he fancies that while bathing, the bathing machine was washed out to sea and to the shores of a beautiful island, whose queen receives him graciously and offers him a crown. To the immense satisfaction of the Court, there is a body of interesting young girls. Out of this situation Mr. Toole contrives to extract unlimited fun by singing two or three excellent songs in capital humour before he awakes. There are some good topical hits, one at the House of Commons, which we are told has power to make and reject laws, "even Bradlaughs."

NEWTON AND EA HL I STOWN. OM= PARADE AT EARLESTOWN.—On Saturday after- noon the first church parade of the Ninth Lancashire (New- ton company of the Warrington Bitallion) Volunteers took place at the Earlestown Parish Church. The company marched from the Cock Pit head quarters, headed by their j brass band under Mr. Hibbert, to the church where a sermon I was preached by the Rev. Gustavus Carson, of Liverpool. ' A very large crowd accompanied the volunteers, and the church was well filled. ACCIDENT TO A JOINER AT NEWTON.-011 Saturday a joiner, named George Kersley in the employ of Mr. Joseph Pennington, contractor, was engaged erecting a high roof at the Newton Paper Mill, when one of the planks of the scaffolding on which Kersley stood cracked and gave way. Kersley, to avoid falling among the machinery, jumped off to the front ground below, unfortunately receiving severe bruises and a serious shaking. Every attention was promptly given to the poor fellow. He was conveyed home and Dr. Handyside was promptly in attendance. His injuries are so I Sacra that it will by several weeks before he will be able to resume work. EARLESTOWN AND DISTRICT LIBERAL CLUB BOWLING GBISES..,—On Saturday a number of the members of the Liberal Club played a very enjoyable handimp on their conveniently-situated bowling green, Houghton-street for small prizes. Over 30 competitors took part in the game. The contest was decided in five heats. The following were the winners in the various heats :—ist heat: Messrs. T. Baxter R. Bennett, P. Critehley, J. Barlow, P. Kenny, J. G. Faulkner, J. Taylor, H. Waywell, C. Kelly, G. Birks, H. Strachan, J. Bothwell, P Mahon. J. Watson, T. Lambert, and J. Whittle. 2nd heat: R. Bennett, G. Birks, J. Both- well, H. Waywell, P. Mahon, IL Strachan' J. Whittle, and J. Taylor. 3rd heat: P. Mahon, J. Rothwell, J. Taylor, and R. Bennett.. 4th heat: R. Bennett and P. Mahon. sth and final heat : P. Mahan beat R. Bennett. The committee are to be complimented on securing a suitable bowling green for the sole use of the members of the club during the summer season. The experiment is in every way success- ful, and keeps the members of the club well together. RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT EARLESTOWN.—EarIy on Tues- day morning a train of 35 laden coal waggons was travel- , ling from Haydock in the direction of Warrington, when, ; owing to some complication of the points, the locomotive and four of the wagons left the rails within a few yards from the junction of the Liverpool and Manchester lines at Earlestown. The engineman and fireman seeing the danger, and having done all they could to bring the train to a stand, jumped off the engine and escaped unhurt. The wheels of the locomotive, and the four wagons immediately following, I sank below the axles into the ground. Information was at once fotwarded to Warrington, and a breakdown gang, under Mr. Mountfield, district locomotive superintendent, was soon at work, and by noon had succeeded in clearing the line The tender of the engine was damaged. The accident did not cause any obstruction to traffic, beyond the stoppage for some time of Messrs. Evans' coal trains.

.. - THE VOLUNTEERS' CHURCH PARADE.—A correspondent writing to us on this subject, says :—" I have nothing to say against the appearance of the men, or of their general conduct, but to hear.the,n led to and from the church ser- vice by the band playing such a silly, senseless, and disgrace- ful tune as "Over the garden wall," accompanied with the words by many of the boys and silly young men following the volunteers, is nothing less than discreditable in the extreme. If this first parade is a sample of what we ark to expect in the future, it will be better for the morals and general character of the in labitants of Earlestown if we never have another. The band might, at least, have given us some respectable music." EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN JUVENILE MISSIONARY A Sbo- - usual quarterly meeting, in connection with the above society, was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, on Sunday afternoon, when there was a fair attendance of scholars and teachers. I have pleasure in stating that I ind tke school in a healthy and satisfactory condition, and all going on quietly and regu- larly. THE WSW AT PRESCOT Ch MEETING OF THE CONGREGATION.

- - On Tuesday a meeting of the congregation of Prescot Parish Church, was held in the chancel for the purpose of forming a committee similar to the one in existence a few year's ago, to consider the best means of improving the musical portions of the services. The Vicar, the Rev. L. W. Sampson, occupied the chair, and there were aleo present the Rev. F. R. Lee (curate), Messrs. W. L. Evans, J.P.; H. Cross, F. H. Hendall, W. Tyrer, T. Evans, A. F. Evans, F Green E. Chrimes, J. K. Slack, T. Prescott, J. J. Brown,and a number of ladies.—The CHAIRMAN remarked thatthey had assembled there to see in what way they could improVe3l, singing in the church, and as Mr. W. L. Evans had con- sidered the subject, be thought they had better get tobisi- ness at once.—Mr. EVANS said there was net a very large attendance of those interested in the musical portions of the services of the church. He was sorry to see that, but hoped it did not correctly indicate the views of the congregation on the subject. It would be in the recollection of many who were present at the last Easter vestry meeting, that before he was elected churchwarden, he indicated what course he should endeavour to take respecting the improvement of the musical portions of the services of the church, if the gentles.' men who were elected as his colleagues, agreed with hill. He was glad that those gentlemen who were elected as is Colleagues did agree with him, and they took it for gran Ana all the members of the congregation were desirous thn =apical portions of the services, should be improved. 1110, course they thought most likely to have that effect was tti. appoint a committee to take in hand the management of that. choir. At present the vicar and the churchwardens wen, responsible for that, and, speaking in their presence, they' were willing, and desirous he might say, to give up their authority to a committee. The churchwardens did :totted themselves competent, in a musical point of view, to msks arrangements for the management of the choir and direct the musical portions of the services of the church. They proposed that a committee to be cal- led the choir committee should be formed. He moved "That a committee be formed consisting of the vicar and churchwardens as ex-officio members, and six other members to take in hand the management of the choir; such com- mittee to have the sante control over the organ, organist, and singers, as the vicar and churchwardens now have." If it was thought desirable to increase or decrease that num- ber, it would be for the meeting to decide. It seemed to him that a committee of eleven persons was quite large enough, and as there was an add number there would always be a majority (if all members turned up) when any difference of opinion arose, without appealing to the chair. As re- gards the organ something required to be done to it, and the organist would probably be able to tell them what it was. The committee would not wish to interfere with the organ- isos province, nor would they have the right to do so any more than the vicar and churchwardens had at present. The real meaning of his motion was that the vicar and church- wardens vacated their position in favour of a committee.— Mr. KENDALL had great pleasure in seconding the motion.— The motion was then put to the meeting and unanimously agreed to.—The committee was then appointed, consisting of the vicar (Rev. L. W. Sampson). and the churchwardens as ex-officio members, and Messrs. F. H. Kendall, F. Green, W. Fryer, F. Smith, Mrs. W. L. Evans, and Miss Coates.— Mr. THOMAS Evsys thought the Rev. Mr. Lee, the curate, should be on the committee, and, after much discussion, Mr. W. L. Evans, with the consent of his seconder, altered his resolution to include the curate therein.—lt was also re- solved that the committee have power to fill up any casual vacancy that might occur.—On the motion of Mr. 3. J. BROWN, seconded by Mr. W. TYRER, a vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman for presiding.—The CHAIRMAN thanked those present, and said it would always be his en- deavour to do everything he could for the improvement of the services. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: CONFIRHATION SERVICES AT HUTTON AND PRESCOT.
div.p: CONFIRHATION SERVICES AT HUTTON AND PRESCOT.

On Wednesday, the Biskop of Liverpool held a confirma- tion service at St. Michael's Parish Church, Huyton, in the presence of a large congregation. Ninety-three candidates were presented, from the following parishes :—lluyon (in- cluding the Quarry), 22 males and 44 females; Roby, 14 males and 12 females; Knowsley, 1 female; total, males 36, females 57. The candidates were as heretofore arranged in the front pews in the middle aisle. The clergy present, in addition to the Bishop, were the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, vicar of liuyton; Rev. W. I. Feilden. vicar of Knowsley and rural dean; Rev. G. J. Banner, vicar of Roby; and the Revs. W. T. Southward and A. T. Warne, curates of Huyton. A hymn having been sung, the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, the vicar, read the preface, after which the Bishop addressed the candidates from the pulpit, particularly impressing upon them the solemnity of the occra.:on and the seriousness of the step they were about to take. The ceremony of the laying on of hands having been performed, the Bishop, in the course of another address, said that the confirmation day in any parish was always a very solemn occasion. Never since th.• world began until now had there been a time when there was so much temptation, which was partly due to the invention of railways and steam navigation, by which people were continually going to and fro, from one end of the land to the other; and partly to the increase of wealth and attrac- tioas. He repeated there never WAS a time when young men and women needed so much advice and warning to take heed what they did lest they made a shipwreck of their immortal souls. The clergy stood on a different place to them, and saw danger where young people could not. The clergy—some of them—had fought their way throngh temptation and knew where there were difficulties and dangers better than they possibly could do. They, therefore, spoke from experience, and he wanted them to stand upon God, and to take heed lest, after being confirmed and making la solemn declaration, they missed the way to eternal life. After exhorting them to conduct themselves with all humility and to lay a firm hold upon Jesus Christ, the I bishop procea-ded to impress upon the Candidates the neces- sity of attending to partake of the Lord's Supper. He appealed to them to come not once only but constantly. He grieved to say a custom was springing up amongst them that if young people went to the Lord's Supper once, or what they were pleased to call their first communion, after being confirmed, they need not go to the Lord's table at all it might be for many, many long years. That was a bad custom, it was an ignorant custom, and one he feared was in the church, and it ought not to be allowed for a moment. the bishop asked the elder persons pjesent, who had been confirmed, to help, assist, and aid the young people in living up to that profession they had made. They must be kind and wise in dealing with them, and if they went back from that profession, to take them gently by the hand and give them friendly warning and encouragement, and try and keep them up to the mark--The last confirmation service was held by the Right Rev. Bishop Kelly, formerly vicar .of Kirkby. In the af.ernoon, the bishop held a confirmation service at Prescot Parish Church. There were present the Rev. W. L. Fielder', Rev. L. W. Sampson, vicar of Prescot, and the Rev. F. R. Lee, curate of Prescot ; and there was also a tolerably large attendance of the parishioners and others. The candidates who offered themselves for con- firmation numbered 74-36 males and 38 females. At the cmclusion of the ceremony the bishop gave A charge to the young people, solemnly impressing upon them the import- ance of the step they had taken, and pointing out the path they ought to take in the future.

Bryan Conroy, 67 years of age, well known to the pohce, residing at Sutton, was charged this mornint, with having caused the death of William Miller, labeurer, resid- ing at the same place, on Saturday .evening, the 14th of May. They met in Norman's-road, and deceased said to the prisoner, "Will you have a glass ? " Prisoner replied, "No, I will not. I will go home." "Very well," said the deceased, "I will go and have one myself." Prisoner got into a temper and said, "Do you mean to insult me in that was, at Iheokime time seizing him and throwing him, down, his head coining in contact with a brick wall. Ills head was ieviriily-cnt. Deceased got up, and prisoner said, " Will We another swing." beceased then, -struck the -planner in the face, and prisoner again threw. him against the 'same wall. They struggled a long time on the grohntl, and people were pre- vented from interfering by 'prisoner's dog, which growled and bar!;ed timely. Eventually a soman separated the men. A CHILD SC.ALDED TO DEATH AT ST. HHIHNH-00 Monday evening, a child, one year and nine months old, died from the effects of scalds. Deceased was the daughter of John MeEwen, a glass bottle maker, residing at 14,, King-street, Windle. About seven o'clock on the evening lof the 10th, the mother was in the kitchen washing herself, when the child ran from the street against the handle of x pan containing boiling water placed on the fire, and knocked it on to the floor. Deceased was severely scalded on the right side and left knee. The mother immediately turned round, and seeing the condition the child was in, despatched a messenger for Dr. Twyford, who sent some lotion and directions for its use. - The lotion was applied, and the child carefully attended to, but death took place on Monday [evening. On Thursday an inquest was held at the Peels' Arms, before Mr. Driffield, coroner, and a verdict of "acci- dental death "returned.

Si. HELENS LIBERALS AT THE COVNTY SEAT OF Mn. OLLOBTORL—On Thursday morning about 38 members and I friends of the St. Helens Liberal Club went on their annual plaids, which, like last year they held at llawarden, per- mission having been obtained from Mr. Gladstone' enabling them to visit the new and old castles, the gardens, grounds, and other places of interest to be seen there. The Afirty atgirted by the 10-28 train to Chester, And had an enjoyable thnner at the Albion Hotel is that town. ;They went in coaches and other vehicles to ign, seven miles distance where they, put the Old Glynn Arms Hotel, which has been ~.vnnovated and specially adapted for the accornmo- -4.45i. excursionists. The visitors were shown through the woods and private grounds, visited the old castle, au& • bad glimpses into the rooms of the new castle. Rain coding on, they burrried back to the hotel, where they waited until the weather became favourable for starting on their journey; and they had a delightful drive back to Chester and partook of a eubstantial tea at the Albion Hotel. The party waa under the guidance of Mr. A. F. Muir, who arranged the plc-nic.

I have also used It at sports to time sprint races, and may say that it timed as accu- rately as Twenty-five Guinea Watches used for the same par- pose.--Y.urs faithfully, JAS. T. TITHER.

CONFIRMATION SERVICE AT BT. HELSNII.—On day morning the Bishop of Liverpool held a confirmation service in the Parish Church, which was filled. About 320 candidates—the majority of whom were females—from the various churches in, the immediate neighbourhood pre- sented themselves for confirmation. After the ceremony had been performed the Bishop, addressing the congrega- tion, said one must have a very cold heart indeed who could not be deeply impressed at the sight of over 300 young persons coming forward for confirmation. When he knew the world they lived in, and what influences were at work., he felt a deep desire to say something which would be of use to them in their future life. They might never meet again in this world, for there never was such a time when people were scattered as the present. Partly by the inven- tion of railways, and paray by steam navigation, the world was continually going to and fro; and very few of them had the burial service read over them in the same place in which they were baptised. But they would all meet at the judgment seat of Christ in that great day when the trumpet would sound and the dead be raised; and bishops, clergy, and congregation would be represented there. He fervently prayed that, none of the candidates who had presented themselves for confirmation that day wouid,be found on the left hand. The candidates bad pledged themselves before that congregation, before the clergy and bishop, and, above all, in the sight of God, with God's help to live the life of Christians. If it was discreditable to turn their backs upon the temperance pledge how much more discreditable and disgraceful after they had taken that pledge that day, "5 it to go with the multitude and turn their bacits upon Christ? God grant that they might be able to look lAric with pleasure upon the 24th May, 1881. He then exhorted then, to be humble when they left the church, and to no home and to their places of work with . a deep sense of their own weakness, and not to put trust in their own strength and good resolutions. He entreated them to attend to the means et grace and the communion, and bade them beware as to the choice of their companions. They had no occasion to be afraid of what they had dono that day. He exhorted them to be courageous' in doing what was right; but ctuu- kenness and dishonesty they ought to be ashamed of. Be appealed to the congregation to sympathise with the candi- dates, and when they found one to err, to speak a kind word in B,,ason, and encleavottr ca draw him gently back into the right path,

All through tho debate on Wednesday the " House was very near entering upon the discussion of which is droner a constitutional question—whether it is the duty of a Government Whip to keep a Howe for private mem- bers as well as for Government., Even Sir Stalford Northcote, although not one of his party had been present to be counted, seemed to imply that the Government ought to have done something. 'and Lord Kensington, Lord Richard Grosvknor, Sir Arthur Flayter, and Mr. Cotes will be cherishing affection for Mr. Bingar, in return for the implied criticisms to which his playfulness has subjected Ahem. If Government whips are to be always ' responsible for a House, and the House contains Mr. Biggar, the duties are even more onerous than is usually believed, and the next step on the part of the whips .will he to incite to a revolt against the count out rule. Judging. froin Wednesday's debate, the materials for raising such a revolt will be easily collected.

RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS AT CHURCE.—The Runcorn volunteers attended service at the Parish Church on Sun- day morning, when an. appropriate sertribn *was preached by the Rev. Canon Barclay from Hebrews xi' c, 34—" Waxed valiant .fight, and turned to flight the armies of the aliens." ' ...

WIDNES MILTON CHM= BAND OE Hopp. —OD Tuesday evening, a public meeting was held in connection with the Milton •Conwe thae 1 ChttrehY Sunday School Band of Hope, uud-r the preildenci of the key. T. Peters, the pastor. An interesting prpgraname was,gone,through by the children.

Aannum.kknumNmnNT Larson= OF FOLD= AT ST. HELENg.—The inspecting officer, Captain Hon. C. G. Legge, Governntent inspector for the Northern District (ac- companied by Captain Alison, the deputy chief constable of the county), made his annual inspection of the police at Sr. Helens, on Wednesday. The Mayor (Alderman J. Har- rison) was present. There were on parade Superintendent Johnston, Inspector Wood, seven sergeants, and forty con- stablos. After a minute inspection a the clothing and ap- pointments, the men were drilled by Sergeant Calliater, after , which the inspecting officer visited the constables quarters, lockups, and other portions of the station. He then entered the office and inspected the books, and found no fault with anything.

MELnoratrz Exnrarrzcay.—We learn that Messrs. Gelding, Davis,' and C 0.., Limited, alkali manufactures of Widnes and Liverpool, have been awarded a silver mddal of the above exhibition for the superior excellence of their caustic soda and bleaching powder. The same firm also•ob- tained a first award at the late Sydney Exhibition. Lemma AT RUNCOMQ.—On Saturday, a yacht, about 40 feet in length, which had been built by Mr. Wilson Littler, was launched on the Bridgewater canal, from the •yard of Mr. Leech, near the Sprinch. The vessel was named the Heather Bell. As she went down the ways, two rnen, ' who were assisting, had to jump Into the canal in order to escape injury.

BEEAICINO INTO' A DWELLING- DLOUSE, IT RUNCORN. --At- ME' Cheshire Quarter Sessions on Wednesday, Ann Woffenden (35), factory worker; John smith (38), labourer; Margaret Jones alias Smith (29), charwoman; Ellen Coffey; (21), servant; and Robert Barker (1.8), labourer, indicted for breaking and entering the dwelling-house of VVilliam More- ton, at Rnncorn, and stealing various articles ef clothing and ornaments, and with receiving the same, were cachsentenced to nine months' imprisonment with hard labour. TICE LATE WIDNES CONCERT.-Mr. A. Speakman writes :—"The coneert in aid of JamesTtean (who is suffer- ing from paralysis) resulted financiallyas follows—Received for tickets of admission, £l2 75.; received for programmes, Gs..9d.—£l2 13s. 9d. Paid for printing, rent of room, dm., £3 78.; total, £9 Os. 9d. The committee beg to thank all •whein any way contributed to the success of the concert.. The chairman, the excellent orchestralohand, the handbell ringer* and all the ladies and gentlemen responded very readily to thecommittee's appeal fut. help, and Shay were seconded by a generous public, who purchased tickets and so helped the affair „pp." . . RECOGNITIOR SERVICES AT WIDNES.-Mr. T. Carver, the newly appointed pastor to the congregation worshipping in the Baptist Chapel', Butchinson-street, 'Widnes, received a welcome from the congregation and the ministers of the other Nonconformist churches in town, on Thursday even- ing. A tea meeting, to which some 80 persOns sat down, took place prior to the recognition services, at which Mr. Edward Mounsey, of Liverpool. occupied the chair. • Ther,l were also present the Revs. T. Peters (Cong,reptionalisti), C Bingant, and J. Tesseyman (VVesleyans); Messrs. . C. Farrie, Carey, Miller, dm. Addresses welcoming Mr. Carver to his pastorate, were delivered by several of the above gentleman, some of reborn spoke on the duty of the church in relation to the pastor, and gave some sound advice to the church on this subject. Mr. Carver, briefly replied, thank- ing the speakers for their cordial welcome, stating•his readi- ness to help his brother ministers either on the platform or in the pulpit, expressing his desire to follow the advice of the Apostle, to ." Live praceably with all men," and es- pecially the tninistersof the neighbourhood,and concluded by soliciting the earnest co-operation of the members and their' sincerest prayers. ~ , .

AGRICT7LTIIRAL PROSPECTS IN LANCASIIIRE AND CHEs- uram.—A Joirespondent writes:—" I save rarely seen vege- tation make such i leap as it has done during the last week or ten days. • If the present rate of growth be maintained grass will be ready' for the scythe about the average date. Already grass has found its way Into the market. Ever- greens, which suffered so keenly by the cold winds of Jan., are recruiting very much better than, might have been expected. Everywhere that I have noticed, both" in Lan- cashire and Cheshire, the orchards .are very promising for bloom of all sorts, and the frosty nights of last weak and the high winds of this do not appear to have done the blossom much damage. I notice that . the ash and the oak trees are more equal in the development of their foliage than usual, so that according to the old-time theory of pre dieting the weather by these trees, we should have .a fine summer. In a bug walk through a ploughing district I have noticed on very, dry soils more, corn grub-eaten than might have been expected, and some fields of grain, both oats and wheat. very uneven. Ploughed lands have not yet recovered the effects of the bad seasons, and 'same are very foul with weeds. Potato .planting is nearly complete. Clover is looking pretty well, and is growing last, bpt the rye grass which bas,come under my ohrervation is thinly rooted. In the-dairying districts of North Lancashire. where there has been. little Or no cattle disease, Many mulch vie's have turned out to be drapes '.,,that is, QUI. of calf—which will be a loss, but the farmers are more hopeful of the future."

MEETING OF RUNCORN CREDITORS.—OD Tuesday, meeting of the creditors of the estate of Mr. John Knowles, was beld at Wilson's Hotel. The liabilities were stated to be £1,200, and the assets, subject to the realisation of a 'bill of sale about £3OO. fs,o offer being made, liquidations was resolved upon, and Mr G. J. Knight, chartePed accountant, ii.nd Mr. J. W. Lightburn, were appointed trustees, with a committee'of inspection of four, and the principal creditors. A WIDNES INQUEST. —On Saturday an inquest was held at the Cornmeicial Inn, Widnes, by Mr. C. E. Driffield, county coroner, on the body of an unknown woman, who was found in the Mersey, near Widnes Marsh, on Thursday week, under circumstances reported in the last issue of the • Examiner. The evidence did not throw anyyriew ,light on the identity of the deceased, and the jury returned an open verdict. • THE RUNCORN BOWLING CLUB AT HALE. The other day six rwornbe'rs of the Runcorn Bowling Club visited the Childe of Hale Hotel, Hale, and. joined in a game, of bowls with eleven local men. They were successful in carrying away all the prizes, three in number.. Mr.,R. Wright and Mr. Jno. Price were left in to play off the final tie, but night coming 'on prevented what would no doubt have concluded a good game. The prizes were £1; '2lld, 10e.; and 3rd, 4s.

.140 ED BEACONSFIELD AND LANOASIIIRE *Tomtes.—A serious charge is made against the Lancashire Tories. It was well known that the appearance of Mr. Whitley's bathing countenance lured Lord Beaconsfield on thd rocks of a false security, and induced him to lay down the authority which was removed from his reacfi for ever. The story new runs, however, that not only was it a Lancashire Tory who beguiled the then Prime Minister into dissolving Parliament at the wrong time, but that it was also Lancashire Tories who hindered him from dissolving at the right time. We hare been told in some of the bitmraphies of Lord Beacons- field that at an important period of his late official career he was thwarted by his colleagues and compelled to give Way rather than break op the Cabinet. It is well known that, efter the return of the plenipotentiaries from Berlin,-in :u v. 1878, the Liberals expected, or rather feared, that Is i Beaconsfield would appeal to the country to ratify his or ign pollee,. Parliament had then run five sessions-'-a lair airerage life; and the Prime Minister was in the zenith of his power. But month after month passed away; no dis- solution name; and the Liberals noted the fact that the tide Of Ministerial favour, having reached its height, began to recede. The Govet nment majority in the Commons, which wee 143 on the Berlin Treaty in August, fell to 101 on the Afghan warm n December; and in the following March on the Zulu wart was 00.: In the abort space of seven months it hid lessened lw more than one-halt of the subservient assembly. People were becoming weary of war upon war, and honour with peace had long before disappeared. Then the disastrous season of 1872 further crippled trade and destroyed agrieulture; so that, when the dissolution came, in March, 1880, the nation was ripe for a change and speedily effected it. But why did not such an astute-tacti- cian as Lord Beaconsfield take advantage of the popular tide in 1878,'seize it at its flood, and mecum a sea-ond lease of power? It le understood that the most persistent opponent of a dissolution at that time was Sir Richard Cross, who was joined by two other Lancashire members in the Cabinet —Celonel Stanley and Viscount Sandon. Their contention I was that the prospects of .reviving tra4e would be shattered by a dissolution just Or nit,airl they made sure of retaining I their authority whenever an appeal to the country was made. The result was the utter destruction of the Tory power. It is not always true that what Lancashire says on one day England says on the morrow. . . . THE FATAL A CCIDNNT AT WARRINGTON.—An inquest was held at the Woolpack rnn, Sankey-street, on Monday, by Mr. C. -WIDNES BAPTISTS.—The Baptists of Widnes have for some time been under a cloud, but it is to be hoped that there are brighter days in store for thent, now that they may, in BOW, sense, be said to be affiliated to the great church at the Metropolitan Tabernacle, where there are upwards of 4,000 members. ,This connection hat been brought about by, Mr. T. Carver, of Mr. Spurgeo'S'College, being appointed -to the pastorate. The ret. gentleman, tvho is highly spoken of, commenced his "ministry on Sunday last, when there were good congregations. WIDNES WORKMAN lIBLIC-HOUSE COMPANY—At an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of this company, held on Thursday, in the Cocoa-rooms, Hutchin- son-street, it was decided to wind up the affairs of the com- pany by voluntary liquidation. Great regret was expressed that an institution having such worthy objects in view could not have been carried on in Widnes with commercial success, and special expressions of sympathy were made to the working classes, and whose shares had been taken up in the hope that their, investments might not only prove re munerative, but also assist in promoting tile comfOrt and sobriety of the community. LECTURE AT PENKETIL—On Monday a lecture, on India arid the Afghan war, was delivered in the Assembly-room, Penketh, b Sergeant Laverack, of Leeds. The chair'was occupied by Mr. Garnett, and there was a large audience. The lecturer, who has served with the Path regiment in indis 17 years, graphically depicted a soldier's life, described the manners and customs of the Indian people, ,and made some interesting remarks upon their country. He exhibiteJ Idioramic views of Indian scenery, and some of the more re- markable places. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was accoriled.to Sergeant Laverack for his interesting lecture. In the afternoon there bad been an exhibition to the children of the schools in the township.

SAD DEATH OF AN OLD MIN NIUE Mr. J.-E. J.-E. Worsley, deputy coroner, held an inquest e' the Red Lion Inn, Preston-o'-th'-liill, on Saturday, on the body of William Rosbotfom who met with such injuries from a fall on Thursday as to cause his death the following day. It appeared that deceased was 86 years of age, and-lived at Aston. He had been nearly blind for about four years past. He was found by a boy lying on the highway, near Fred- sham, on Thursday evening, covered with blood, having evidently fallen from an eminence by the side of the read about ten feet high. The lad gave information to a man named Joseph Hallmark, who had the deceased conveyed home. He waS attended by Dr. Robinson, but he died the next day. According to the medical testimony, the left shoulder and one of the fingers had been dislocated. Severe internal injuries had also been sustained, and deceased had vomited blood shortly before he died. A verdict of death froln injuries received from a fall was returned. _

REFERENCE TO Tint REVISED Nat. TESTAMENT AT ST. HELENS.—The Rev. R. J. Ward (St. Helens) on Sunday read from and preached on the subject of the revised version: He might say there perhaps had never been a time when the eyes of the whole English-speaking world had been fixed with such interest on the Bible. The design of the revision ,had been to get and bring out the real meaning of the Word of God. Everybody felt that it was too sacred to be tam- pered with by heedless hands, but so such bands bad been employed, and the New Testament had come back to na not dyed in colour, but just clean. • Deficiencies bad been removed and inaccuracies corrected, and they might be more ' certain than ever that they had now got the very Word of God. It had stood the test of the first scholars of the time, and every preacher must feel that the revised ver- sion waa a great boon to himself and a very great benefit to his people.

THE LANCASHIRE Hussaus.—The prizes for the best swordsmen in the Lancashire Hussars, who are at present assembled at Southport for their annual eight days' drill, were awarded on Wednesday. The competition was very keen, many well-known military geßtlemen present remark- ing that they never saw a better display in any other yeomanry regiment. The following were the successful competitors :—A troop (Ashton-in-Mackerfield): 1, Private Thomas Holker ; 2, Private George Boon; 3, Private Thos. Pendlebury. B Troop (Moss Bank, St. Helens): 1, Private Joseph Sefton; 2, Corporal Wilson; 3, Private W. Critchley. C Troop (Newton-le-Willows): 1, Private Thos. Bradcleck ; 2, Private H. Wheeler; 3, Sergeant Glover. D Troop (Ormskirk and neighbourhood): 1, Sergeant Draper; 2, Private Aspinall; 3, Sergeant Banks. The prizes are—for the first in each troop; £3; for the second, it 10s.; and for the third, 10s. The first in each troop afterwards competed for the regimental prize of £5, which was won by Sergeant Draper, of the D Troop.

SLAIN BY DRINK AT RUNCORN. On Thursday morning, an enquiry was heir( at the Masonic Hotel, Run- corn, by Mr. Worsley, deputy coroner, as to the death of a man named Hanry Walsh, aged 27. who was found in a dying condition in a stable at the Top Locks on Tuesday, and who died a few hours after his removal to the house of I his mother in Regent-street. The deceased was a tiatrnan by occupation, but during the last two ye trs and a half he had been very irregularly employed, and had only managed to sustain himself in what he had earned by helping boats up the locks. He was stated to have injured himself some three months ago by lifting too great a weight in Liverpool. He came home ill last Friday week, but afterwards went away, and was not seen until the Tuesday morning, when I he was found in Mr. Crosby's stable, Top Locks, lying on a wheelbarrow half filled with straw. He was breathing very very heavily, and appeared to be dying. P.C. Demons went to Mr. Wright, relievisg officer, about the poor fellow, and also fetched Dr. McDougall, who did all he could to assist deceased; but he died about one o'clock the same day. He had been a man of very irregular habits, much addicted tQ drink, and for some time the lodging-house keepers had refused to receive him owing to his filthy habits. The jury returned a verdict of died fromnatural causes, and ' plid a high compliment to P.C. Bossons for the activity lie had displayed in trying to do all he could to assist the deceased.

ACTION AGAINST A. PILOT ST A. RUNOOIIN FIRM.-At the Liverpool County Court, on Monday, before Mr. Thom- pson, Messrs. Brundritt and Co., ship owners and quarry proprietors, sued Thomas Lewis, a Liverpool licensed pilot. for £2l lOs., being the amount of damage sustained by the plaintiffs' schooner, The John, in consequence ot a collision with the steamship Spartan, while the latter was in charge of the defendant. On the 28th December last, while the plaintiffs' schooner, which is 62 tons register, was proceed- ing up th 3 river in a fair wind, a little to the eastward of mid-channel, the Spartan came out of the Alfred Dock, :it Birkenhead, stern foremost, and was right across the bows of the schooner when the two vessels were from seventy to one hundred yards apart. The steamer was in charge of the defendant Lewis, who is a licensed pilot. When the schooner was about twenty yards from the steamer, the master of the former starboarded his helm, to try and avoid the collision which he saw was inevitable;. but. almost at the same mo- ment the engines of the steamer were reversed, and she went full speed ahead, the intention being to clear the bows of the schooner. However, the two came into collision, the stern of the steamer slightly, damaging. the starboard fore rigging of the smaller craft. It was stated by the plaintiffs' witnesses that the collision could have been avoided if the steamer had gone ahead sooner; and by those for the defence that the schooner had ample time to steer clear of the steamer when she was first seen, considering that there wos a good sailing wind. His Honour said there appeared to have been a miscalculation on both sides, and he there- fore found for the defendant.

CATTLE DisEasx x Cursmag.—At the Knntsford Quarter Sessions Captain Arrowsmith, chief constable for county, stated to the Executive Comtnittee of the Local Authority that since the last Quarter Sessions, held on the 4th ult., foot-and-month disease had appeared in five places, and 104 animals bad been attacked, of which number four died, one was killed, 73 recovered, and 26 remained under treatment. On the 19th inst. a case of pleuro-pneumonia (the first since October last) was reported front Stayley, in the Hyde division. Captain Arrowsmith presented a return showing the satisfactory working of the Contagious Dis- eases (Animals) Act. The compensation paid yearly by the local authority for the destruction of diseased animals, com- mencing with 1873, was £286, £715, £553, £636, £l5l, £6OB, £506, £241, and for seven months ending March last £33. From fhe let of October, 1878, compensation was allowed for healthy animals slaughtered which had been in contact with cattle affected with pleurn-pneumonia; in 1879 £667 was allowed for this purpose and in the following year £B5, making the total of compensation for the period £4,483. The expense in veterinary surgeons' fees, printing,,inspectors' expenses, ire, for the period was £3,015.
