div.p: LOCAL NOtE.S,

No doubt that most of my readers • have something to say at tines upon the difficulty of early rising. Either their watches are too fast or too slow,, or the servant girl over- sleeps herself and knocks at one's door. an hour after the prescribed time, of the alarum gets out of order and upsets our nervens system by going off just as we have settled into a peeceful slumber. The other morning about five o'clock! siw an old man in his shirt sleeves walking from dedr to door and knocking his neighbours up. until he had raised about two dozen of them, being double the number of those who wished him to do so, the probability being that those who wished to continue their slumbers for another hour Or two rearded the old gentleman, when•engaged on this mis- sion of charity, as an intolerable nuisance. It is therefore no small consolation to hear that the problem-of securing early riSing has at last been solved. The telephone is the medium through which this happy result has been attained. At Liege the authorities notify. that subscribers may have telephones fixed in -their, bedrooms, and by this means be called at any hour of the day or night by an official in charge at the central office. This is not a bad idea, but. I hope that when the authorities et this town adopt it they will be able to emsure for their official an individual who is not a practical, joker, or I fear, that we they find it not always an unmixed good. I hear, it is rumoured, that a monstre excursion is to be, promoted on Whit-Monday from St. Helens and Warrington to Runcorn, in order to witness the grand review of the Salvation Army which is to take place on that day. My informant states that all the officers, and many of the rank and file who will take part in the proceedings will he mounted on donkeys. lam unable to vouch for the accu- racy of the statement, but if it is correct no'cloubt much amusement will result from seeing these gentlemen mounted on such sph Red chargers. The day has coma at last in whieli the publicans and, the Good Tempters bare been able to meet on- ono common platform. They have been lately engaged in slaughtering a dead horse—Mr. Gladatone's proposal for licensing rail- way carriages for the sale of intoxicating drink. It is curious to notice, too, that they both advance the same ob- jection to passengers being allowed to take wine or, ,birter beer ' with their dinner in a Pullman car, viz, that there are :plenty of refreshment rooma and licensed houses at which travellers can obtain refreshment without having it supplied to thent in trains. Tile opposition of the teetotallers is quite consistent additionalwi t their facilities acm d pb eo ni egy 0, ffwerheidchthise tBo ritriosthe s tptia lai pinyen sf for r en. taining intoxicating drink. On the other hand, the British publican is rejoicing because that in future, as in the past, thirsty souls will have to fill their flasks and bottles before starting on a journey.

That little pest to business men generally, the fonrpenny bit, is to sink into oblivion! The Master of t4e Mint re- marking that no fourpenny piece has been coined since 1856, says that the coin continues to be withdrawn in con- siderable quantities, and that it will shortly Cease to circulate altogether. I don't think that anyone will regret the fact. The disappointment in many quarters will, be that threepenny bits are not also to be banished to the limbo of things that were. There does not appear to be any chance of this, however, notwithstanding that the bank authorities have complained bitterly of being flooded with them by church, chapel, and charitable officials. Nearly two millions of threepenny pieces have been set afloat in. a single year ; and so longas the church, chapel, and mission rooni'collection is popular, they eill, I presume, continue to have a hod upon the national affections. They represent the minimum price at whit.h respectable godliness can nom-, ply with conventional requirements.

A curious age,was heard at the St. Helens County Court this week, in which Mr. Adam Gibson endeavoured to per- suade Mr. William Burns to pay for Mrs. Burns's wedding dress, but failed. Judge Thompson told the plaintiff that be should be very careful in trusting a woman for her wed- ding dress, because on the day of her marriage she was relieved from the responsibility of paying for it. After this it is more than probable that Mr. Gibson will act upon his Honour's advice, as he does not appear to habe been very willing to present Mrs. Buns with her wedding "suit." The case is one which I have no doubt other tradesmen will profit by, unless they intend to make presents of wed- ding dresses to their fair customers. The judge asserted that if defen4ant promised to pay it was only a debt of honour, and as Mr. Gibson has failed to recover the cost of the dress by legal means he will now have to rely upon defendant's honour. It remains to be seen how much honour defendant 18 possessed of, aid whether Mr. Burns does not think that his wife is worth a wedding dress, although he bad no money or property with her, and, as it is five years since the wedding took place, he has had plenty of time to find out what she is really worth.

_ Men purposely take upon themselves to shuffle off the mortal coil for many strange reasons, but it is not often we hear of a man committing suicide because he is the unhappy possessor of a superfluity of this world's goods. Such ap- pears to have been the case with an elderly gentleman lately residing in London, who hanged himself to a beam in an outhouse. It was stated at the inquest that whenever he went to receive dividends or purchase property he became very despondent, and in one of these despondent moods he terminated his career. This was the sad result of acing upon the prompting:4 of his own mind instead of seeking friendly advice. If he had only sought he could easily have found a friend who would have shown him how Co dispose of his superfluous wealth 80 as to ease his overburdened con- science very quickly, or if there was any difficulty in doing so in the metropolis lam sure he would have found no diffi- culty in this town. The untimely end of this poor gentleman I fear, however, will not very much check the eager race for wealth. Many persons, on the contrary, will regret all the more that they do not suffer from his com- plaint. FLACCUS.

army stations for May. r CONITEMATION AT WIDNES BY THTt or o Livan- E POOL.—On Tuesday afternoon the ,Right Reverend Lord Bishop of Liverpool held a c St• Mary's onfirmation at J. Church, Widnes. Amongst those present were the Revs. : fi Wright Williams, vicar ; A. Duggan, curate; and George Holloway, vicar of Farnwortb. The church was crowded The candidates numbered 35 females and 36 males. Pre- vious to the service the Bishop said he was going to ask the candidates a very solemn question, and one which he hoped none of them would answer without first seriously thinking what they were about to do. It was whether they were prepared to take upon them the vows made for them at their baptism by their godfathers and godmothers. When they were baptised they were merely little children, and did I not understand what was being done for them. They were brought to the font, and water poured upon them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, and it was then promised for them that they should renounce the world, the ficsh, and the devil ; and, that they would en- deavour to keep God's holy commandments, and walk in the same all the days. of their lives. On submitting to the solemn rite of confirmation, they must make up their minds that, by the help of God, they would try to live Christian lives, and renounce the pomp and vanities of this wicked world, He hoped that they would prove true soldiers of the cross, and not be ashamed of their colours. His lord- ship then proceeded with the sermon, and offered up the usual prayer. He afterwards gave an address to the candi- dates by way of encouragement. He advised them not to forget their bibles, never to be careless in the matter 'of prayer, ard to try to cultivate a spirit of meekness and of humanity; to be ashamed of drunkenness, of gambling, of Sabbath breaking, or of turning their backs upon the house of God.—Mr. Crawford presided at the organ, and played at the opening one of Haydn's voluntaries,and ass concluding voluntary, the Apes Dei, from Mozart's first mass.

The loss of life by the capsizing of the steamer Victoria, near London (Ontario). is, unhappily, much greater than was stated at first:— As early as Wednesday_ evening 238 bodies had been recovered, and it is feared that many others /Were &tangled in the Woodviorkt the sunken vessel. The disaster has thrown the whole province into _ mourning. • A correspondent at Athens telegraphs that the Ministry will in all probability, assume the responsibility of ratifying the Convention with Turkey without summoning the Chamber of Deputies. There are rumosrs of dissensions in the Cabinet, but it is believed that the majority will take the coarse indicated, and ask for a bill of indemnity after- wards. .
I The Budget Committee of the French Chamber of De- puties, acting in accord with the Government, has voted the suppression of the tax on paper, which now yields annually about £160,000.

The Tullarnore Land League last week'issued a manifesto calling upon the Charleville tenants to assemble and demand a reduction of rent. The tenants, lioweyer, met on Thurs- day, and decided that, as they pay fair rent, they will demand no reduction.

div.head: _ __._... WHOLESALE EVICTIONS IN IRELAND.
div.p: _ __._... WHOLESALE EVICTIONS IN IRELAND.

3,000 WRITS ISSUED.—THE TROOPS DEFIED. A Parliarnentary return just issued shows that the total number of ejectment decrees issued in Ireland at the recent Easter Sessions was 3,003. The total amount of rent in arrears, for which the majority of these decrees were granted, was £79,872.

At GlitkoOlan, county Leitrim, on Thursday, 600 troops collected to protect a bailiff while serving process for rent on the property of Lord Annesley. Thousands of people surrounded them, and their attitude was so violent that the bailiff retired without serving his processes. A special meeting of the executive of the National Land League of Great Britain was held on Thursday, in the Con- ference-room of the House of Commons ; IMr. J. M.Carthy presiding. Resolutions were passed calling on Irishmen in England and Scotland, and Englishmen sympathising with them, to evoke public opinion on the subject of evictions by a series of public demonstrations ; and welcoming the sug- gestion of several representative English working men that they should vitand report on the condition of the districts in Ireland where wholesale evictions prevail. It was re- solved to hold demonstrations in Hyde Park, also at Spenny- moor, Oldham, Middlesborough, and other places.

THE EVICTION OF HIGHLAND CROFTERS. The Scotch members are much divided on the merits of the intended motion of Mr. Fraser Macintosh, to prevent fiirther eviction of Highland crofters. Whilst approving in substance of the proposition to put a stop to evictions of the poorer class,of tenants, many of the Scotch members deem the isiue has been raised hi an importunt manner. div.head: CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE
div.p: CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE
SOCIETY. ST. PAUL'S BRANCH.

. . - A successful gathering of the members of thi St. Pau Branch of the Church of England, Temperance Society too place in the Infant School, Heath Side, Warrington, on Monday evening. The Rev. S. Wilkinson, vicar, presided, and in addressing the meeting remarked that the subject of temperance was one of the most important and practical que,its of the day. The Government seemed to be taking that view, and welt legieNting to a great extent 011 the drink traffic. Some time agZ public-houses in Scotland and, Ireland were closed on the sunday, and af. the preeant time there was a motion before the House of Commons to do the same for Wales. He had no doubt that when the time came most members would heartily support the motion. He be- lieved that the publicans would be the that and foremost to welcome the measure, because a great number of them felt it a great hardship upon then, to have to work seven days in the week, and not to have one day'srest. They felt that by not being able to attend God's hue on Sunday they were doing harm to themselves and to their farniffee. Not only publicans, but employers of labour would be glad to see public-houses closed OR the Lord's Day. They had met that evening in connection with the Warrington Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society. There were many people connected with the society who were not teetotalers or absolute abstainers, but the suclety embraced all parties who were anxious and willing to encourage the great virtue of temperance, and to do away with the great vice of drunkenness. It had the sympathy and the help of all lovers of temperance, whether they were absolute ahstaipera or as they were called moderate driuLers. All were engaged in one great work, and that was to stem the torrent of drunkenness which did so much harm in this country. (Applause.) Mr. Armors, in proposing the following resolution : " That it is desirable that every person in this room who is not already a member of the St. Paul's branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, should became so before the meeting closes," said. he believed they were thoroughly convinced that there bad been a necessity and that there still was a necessity for a Church of England Temperance Society in Warrington. He had-the authority of one of the greatest dignitaries of the Church in saying that intem- perance was the parent of mmay other vices; and they had only to look in their daily papers to see that this was a fact. The judges said that were it not for alcohol, nine-tenths of our gaols would have to be shut up; and the superintendents of the lunatic asylums said it was drink which for the most part filled these institutions. Sir William Gull, the eminent physician, when examined before the Lords Commissioners. Said that people were poisoned day by day without knowing it; while Sir John Kaye told them one of the most thrilling passages of his history, how on September 14th, 1857, after terrible hardships and anxieties and almost unequalled deeds of daring the English succeeded in bursting into Delhi, and so for the first time visibly rolling back the bugh tide of Sepoy rebellion. Yet, at that awful moment when half the work had still to be done, when to stand still would be danger, and to recede ruin, the next day was a miserable blank. Why? Because with diabolical ingenuity the Sepoye and people of Delhi, fatally acquainted the English weakness, while they turned out of town, with silver and gold jewels left that deadly fatal kind of property which we, alas! had introduced, and made common in India—ardent spirits. Our soldiers fell into the horrible snare. They plunged wildly into drunkenness; on that day, the English army was practically helpless. Referring to the Society's branch as represented that efening, the speaker said that even the publicans sent their children to them. And that showed they were not against them, but were desirons that their children should grow up in the principles of tem- perance. (Applause.)

Mr. THOMAS MORRIS seconded the resolution, and said he used to think that Acts of Parliament could not make men sober ' • but he now began to think differently, for even a casual observer could see that there was less drunkenness now than when public-houses were kept open late at night and early in the morning. There was not one in twenty, whether man or woman, who got drink because he or she liked it. He had no hesitation in Saving, though, that 19 out of 20 got drunk to enable them to fay other sins they committed on that of intemperance. Cocoa rooms had a tendencyto diminish drunkenness. Working- men must occasionally go somewhere to spend an evening from kome , and a man who had only three halfpence or twopence in his Pocket could spend it in coffee or cocoa. Publicans would not like to see a man stay in his house for an hour or more and only spend twopence. Ile believed in being temperate in all things; he did not ge to excess either in eating or drinking, or anything cleat. All these things were both good and evil, as they were used. If people found that they could not drink without going to excess, his advise to them was that they should ask Ged to help 'them to resist temptation, and he felt sore he would help them in their endeavour to do that which was right and just. (Applause.) Bowro supported the resolution, and said In the posi- tion which he held he had often to speak strongly to the children when they bad been invited out to different places. There was a desire with many people to press drinks upon them, which he c nsidered very improper for children to. take. He had always set hitt face aga:nst them, and he did not like them to be made use of. Be believed that every member of his family was a teetotaler, and he hoped that he would set them an example of temperance, as Mr. Morria had said, in all things. (APPlanl'9) The resolution was carried. Several hymns and recitations were given during the evening by the younger members of the society in a very creditable manner.

The agent asked the manager if he f tke agent) had ever served them with any written notices to repair the landlord's cottage water pipe.. Jrc. In about two or three .ninutes the clerk returned, and with a sneering laugh (at which he seemed pretty clever) said," Well, we have new got as far back as last October. However, . be soon found that his two complainants were not to have dust thrown in their eyes, for he was soon told that they were determine I to have this case gone into, and the truth got at. Just then the manager came from his private office and asked the clerk how the case was going, and being: , assured to his satisfaction by this clever functionary that they were right, he determined, I suppose, to steal a march ~ over us, so he said he was determined to have the whole , matter investigated, so that the ag.mt, who so often corn-. pained., might be checked. But is, arid behold, he was • exactly like Paddy when asked how far it was across the common, who said. Ses with the Waterworks manager; it was a shorter cat into an exposition of their own position than it was out again, for in hate ho asked his subordinate a question or two, which threw both of them at sea in a moment. These questions were in refe- rence to an important point in favour of the agent's position, viz., that after notices for repairs required had been served in some cases three and four weeks even had elapsed before they had attended to the work. This they emphatically denied, but the agent bele to his point, provina that the case in question was one, and showed beyond successful contradiction that tied alone WAS the reason be got another plumber, simply looking after the Just interest of his landlord. He also told them he believed the secret of the whole matter was ' that they were working with um smell, and it might be their summer's, staff of men, even in the midst of a keen winter like the last, thereby making a great savine to the company; but this they very strongly denied, and seemed annoyed at the statement being made. However, it tinned out in a few minutes that the manager himself acknowledged that it was no, and that they had advertised for men but could only get ene,so that be said the f act was thelitiataff was insufficient. Then the clerk was run into such a close corner that he had tern- - duce the order which, I believe, was served by the agent on the Waterworks Company on February Ist. When meestioned, the clerk acknowledged under great pressure that they sent a man just to knock cefa pipe up on the sth of Fete-nary; and then comparing those slatee with the dates on the other plumber's bill when he did the work, was just a month and two or three drys from the day on which the order was served, thus proving they were wrong, and that every statement made by the agent was correct, and would have the effect more and more, no doubt, in establishing the fact in the mind of his employer that he had in his agent a man who did his duty, so that the two points so strongly • denied by both manager and clerk were completely upset, and they were brought to the humiliating position to acknowledge their wrong. "Well," said the landlord, "now you have got to this, if you were in the position you say, hard up for men. I consider you ought to be thankful that my agent could and would step in at a time like that to your relief, and find men to do the work: and all that we ask from you now. since I pay you annually to keep my pipes, &c., in repair, that you should refund us the money it has cost." "Oh, dear no," said the manager, "we cannot do anything of the sort." "Well," said the agent, "do you • fake exception to the prices on the bill ?" to which they replied that the charges w. re moderate aria fair, with the exception of one or two little mettere. The agent said the landlord would no doubt agree to allow them to take off the little overcharge, and give him what they could do it for themselves. To this they strongly demurred, saying the agent had no business to hare their pipes meddled with. Then said the agent, "If we serve you with a notice to repair, and You don't attend to it for some weeks, will you take off our water rate the length of time our tenants are without water." "Oh, dear no," said they. Agent: "Then if we lose our tenants in consequence of yes not attending to our work, and the property becomes empty, will you stand the loss to the land'ord on us proving you are the cause?" ceived whilst protecting her face and head.—ln cross- examination, complainant admitted she sometimes lived in a house about 300 yards from the one in question, but she did not live with a man there. She denied waiting upon two tradesmen in the town, since last Monday, to ask to, receipts for furniture in the bouse.—Corroborative evidence was given on behalf of the complainant. —Mr. Lea said he would call 18 or 19 witnesses to prove that no blows were struck; but only three or four were allowed to be called Mr. Lea raised the point of law that the court had no jurisdiction in the case, as the matter was a dispute referring to the ownership of certain goods and chat- tels.—The Bench ruled that they had jurisdiction, and said they had decided to convict.—Superintendent Johnson said Charles Clubb had been committed to pr leen for nine months for breaking into a dwellinghouse and steal- ing a purse therefrom. John Clubb was concerned in the same matter and received similar punishment. He had also been convicted on charges of assault, game trespass, and under the Fishing Act.—Frisoners were each fitted 20s. and costs. Mr. Lees asked if their worships were disposed to grant him a case on the point of law that he had raised, but the application was refused. Tunsnev.—Before Mr. T. Pilkingten. A RUNAWAY HUSBAND CAUGHT.—James Fairhurst Windle, was charged with unlawfully running away from the township and leaving Alice Fairhurst, hie wife' and two children under 16 years of age chargeable to the Union.— Mr. Charles M. Stuart said Fairhurst deserted his wife a long time ago, and she bad been chargeable to the Union since let January, 1881, so that £7 or £8 were owing to the Union by prisoner. It was not so much the repayment of the money the Guardians wished for as punishment adminis- tered to the offender, because desertion was getting very common in the district. It was generally supposed that the prisomer had gone to America, but within the last 36 hours he heard that the prisoner was in the neighbourhood, and he apprehended him under a warrant.—OD being asked what he had to say for himself, prisoner said be "went down to Liverpool and got into bad company; that was all."—Mr. Pilkington : But is it not your duty to support your wife and family; how were they going to do 7—Prisoner: There was the parish.—Mr. Filkington: It's a nice sort of thing for the parish to keep voar wife and family wills you go away. You can get work if you work properly. It's a most disgraceful thing for you.—After a conversation with the clerk, the magistrate asked the relieving officer if the case could not he remanded.—Mr. Stuart preferred the case being dealt with at once, as it would necessitate his attendance there, and his neglect of duties which he could scarcely afford—Tie magistrate (to prisoner): Well,! can't give you more than 14 days, but you richly deserve more.

div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

-------- given with spirit and precision, and showed a high state of proficiency. The sacred song," He wipes the tear from 1 every eye," was sung by Miss Party with much pathos. Miss Joynson gave " Anmels ever, bright and fair" in an accomplished manner. 'A very desirable change was effected by Mr. Hazlehurst requesting the audience to join in the singing or "We sing of the realms of the Vest," and "There is sweet rest in heaven." Mr. Billingsley presided at the organ with tht. taste for which he is so well known. i We compliment this gentleman upon the manner in which his choir did their duty on Monday. At the conclusion Mr. BILLINGSLEY said he had a very pleasant duty to perform, which was, on behalf of all assembled, to propose a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Hazle- burst for his excellent reading. It needed no words of his to describe the manner of his reading; they had all heard it for themselves. This was the third time Mr. Hazlehurst had read the service with the present choir, and each time he had eclipsed his former effort. ' The motion was seconded by the Rev. J. MORTON, and carried unanimously. Mr. Manzatutsr thanked them for the honour they had accorded him, and said he too had a pleasant duty to per- form, and that was to propose a vote of thanks to the choir for the excellent manner in which they had done their Part. - t

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday qternoon. Mr. T. Sutton-Tiremis presided, and there were also present, the Revs. George .Idoilowsy, Thomas Finegan, James Clarke, and Messra`..RiaAsbaw, Deacon, O'Keeffe, and Danby (clerk.)

DISTRICT EDUCATION cox-tarn:E. This committee reported that during April, the number of cases summoned before them was 422, of which 96 were applications for payment of fees, and 326 for contravention of the Education Act. Fees were recommended to be paid in 78 cases, and 17 applications were refused. There had been 16 prosecutions before the magistrates, and a similar number of convictions.—The report of the committee was adopted on the motion of Mr. Deacon, seconded by the Chairman.

t SITES AND =TIMING COMMITTEE. This report was adopted on the proposition of Mr. Deacon, seconded by the Chairman. It stated that the tender of Messrs. Roberts Bros., for repairing and cleaning West Bank Schools at a cost of £9 95., had been accepted. THE PAVING OF WARRINGTON-ROAD BOARD SCHOOLS. A letter was read from the Widnes Local Board, stating the resolution arrived at by them as to the payin and flagging of Warrington-road Board Schools, Previously gre— ported in The Examiner. Mr. DEACON said the arrangement entered into with the Local Board was that the flagging at Simrn's Cross should be executed as compensation for the land given up to them by the School Board, but there was no agreement as to the work at Warrington-road Schools, and it seemed that the Local Board were going to postr ne this for some reason or other. This would make no difference to the Local Board, but it would to the School Board inasmuch as they were being pressed by the Loan Commissioners to close their capital account, and if the work was not done shortly it would have to be paid for out of revenue. If the work was not done at once the better plan would be to postpone it as if tney had to pay it out of revenue it would considerably increase the rates. The CLERK stated that the Board would only have to pay £3OO, or half the cost of. flagging Warrington-road Schools. lie also explained that in 1876 it was decided that the work at Warrington-road should he done, and the landowners had consented to give up certain land on condition that the Local Board would pave the street on either side the road. The CHAIRMAN said he was sure the Bqard did not wish to add to the present heavy burdens of the town if they could possibly avoid it. It was agreed that the Sites and Building Committee should have a conference with the Local Board to see if some arrangement could not be made in the matter.
. , The motion was carried with acclamation. The singing of the Doxology and the pronouncing of the Benediction brought one of the best services of song it has been our lot to hear to a close.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. Mortrair.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. A FAHNWORTH MAN WHO FELL AMoNG ALLEGED ImEvEs.—Thomas McEvoy andlhomas Cunningham, two labourers, were charged with stealing a belt, a purse, and 63. in money, belonging to Mark Casey.—The only evi- dence which the prosecutor was able to give was to the effect that on the previous Sure* night he was at a Farnworth public-house, where he trfkted the prisoner and another man. On going there he had his purse in his left hand trousers pocket, and the bag produced in court belonged to him. He did not remember anything further with the ex- ception of finding himself locked up in Whines police station on Monday morning.—P.C. Nicholson said that on Sunday night, a little after ten, he was standing at the bottom of Farnworth-street, when he saw the prisoners with the prosecutor, whom they were helping along home, as he was, apparently, very drunk. He followed the three at some distance, and saw the two prisoners take Casey down Peel- house lane, a distance of about 60 yards, into a field on the left hand side of the road. Having put the prosecutor into a hollow part of the field, the prisoners began to examine his clothes. He heard Casev call out "Who are you ?" and one of the prisoners said," We are policemen." On going closer to them, he saw the prosecutor upon his back, and the prisoners with their hands in his pockets. One of them dropped half-a-crown, and he asked McEvoy whose money it was. He said he did not know. A similar question was pat to Cunningham, but he made no reply. Near the spot where the struggle had taken place he found the stolen bag and the belt.—The prisoners were committed to the Liver- pool Quarter Sessions for trial. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell (Chairman) and

RESIGNATION OF MR. MARTIN TAYLOR. The CHAIRMAN said a communication had been received from Mr. Marlin Taylor. which be was sure would be heard with regret hy every m•mber of the Board. The CLERK then read the letter, which was as follows : Ditton, has 23rd. 1881 —Dear Sir,—ln consequence of the action taken by my fi.m I cease to be a member of the Widnes School Board ou may be sure it is with very painful feelings that I thus sever inv connection with the Board, and I take this opportunity to thank you, an-I through you every mem- ber and officer of the Board, for the many marks of kindness I have receik ed from you an I from them. While the differences of opinion have been as sharply defined, and the adherence to principles as firmly maintained as is possible amongst any body of men, I do not remember one word of personal bitter- ness during the irs arid half years I have been a member of the Ward. My shortcomings have been many, but I have had no selfish object in view. My aim has been solely for the wel- fare of Widnes and I shall always feel the same interest in the town where I have spent the longest and happiest portion of my fife. I sincerely hope that the dark cloud of commercial depression which is now pas, fog over Widnes will soon give place to brighter skies, and that in all that is good and great ' Widnes may take a foremost place. I think the Bch ,o 1 Board has done a large share towards the attainment of such a de- sirable position, and my best wishes are for the continued sues cess of the R, ard. and every individual member of It.—l re- main, A° , MateriN TAYLOR. The Cumemes, in a speech of some length, spoke in very eulogistic terms of thc great intelligence, ripe experience,. and fearless independence which had always characterised Mr. Taylor's conduct whilst upon the Board, of which he had been a mom e ,be believed since its formation. I :e alluded to the great amount of time-and the careful attention which that gentleman had given to the Board's interests in the early years of its history. Mr. Taylor had played a promi- Dent and most useful part M the educational work of the, town. When we gave up to the foreigner the great advantage of being placed in the best market in the world, that was, up this country, free of any impost, we had a right to demand fair play and to expect the same privileges in return. CHANCERY OF THE COUNTY PALA- TINE OF LANCASTER. A WIDNES CASE. IN SE WELLS AND 9ALLOWAT (LIMIrSD).—ThIS was aI petition, before Vice-Chapcellor Fox Bristowc, on Monday, for continuing under the supervision of the court a volun- tary winding up, for which resolutions bad been duly passed. The company was formed in 1877 for the purpose of purchasing the business of Messrs. Wells and Galloway, chemical manufacturers, at Widnes, and 160 shares of £lOO each were issued, all of which had been fully paid up.. The petitioners were the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, who were creditors fur £1,500, for goods supplied. The resolutions for winding up the company voluntariliy were come to last month, and Mr. Rawson, the chairman of the company, and Mr. Morrison, a shareholder, were appointed liquidators. The Runcorn Company wished the creditors to be represented in the liquidation, and the present peti- tion was presented rezilly for the purpose of obtaining the appointment of two additional liquideors, the persons pro- posed to be appointed being Mr. Charles Wigg, a director of the Runcorn Company, and Mr. W. Bradshaw.—Mr. Thompson appeared in eupport of the petition, and stated that Mr. Rotel', who represented the company, but who was not then in court, did not, as he understood, oppose the ap- plication.—Mr. Clare, on the part of creditors, had, no ob- jection to make to the order, but suggested that perhaps some difficulty might arise from the fact that when the matter was mentioned at Liverpool the petition was ordered to stand over till the 30th of May. Coder these circum- stances, it woad perhaps be better to take the order that day, subject to it being mentioned oh Monday, in case any creditor or shareholder might desire to be heard upon the petition.—The Vice-Chancellor said if Mr. Rawson ,were alive he should not continue his appointment as liquidator, because he objected to an officer of the company acting in that capacity, but as there were to be three other liquidators he was willing to make the order as prayed.—Mr. Thomp- son desired further that a direction 'night be given under the authority of the 151st section of the Companies Act of 1862, that the powers of the liquidators should not be'exer- cised by less than three of their number; otherwise, as two represented the company and two the creditors, a conflict might arise—The Vice-Chancellor made the order as prayed, subject to any objection that might be taken on Monday next.

WHISTON UNITED METHODIST FERN CHURCII.-011 Sunday last, two sermons were preached in the above place ef worship by the Rev. J. Billington, of Runcorn, formerly , of Presca. The rev, gentleman delivered two excellent and thoughtful discourses, the one in the afternoon being on "Train up a child in the way it should go," and the other in the evening, on the parable of the Prodigal Son. There was a large congregation at each service. • Special hymns were sting in a creditable manner by the chair, Mr. Robert Storey presiding at the harmonium. The collections during the day amounted to slightly over, M, which Sum will be devoted to the fund (Or school purposes. It TM proposed to hold a special service on the following Monday evening, but it was unavoidably postponed.

RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT HUTTON QUARET.-011 Wednes- day, a serious accident befell a labourer named William Robinson, about 60 years of age, awl in the employ of the fiuyton Quarry Iron Works Compiny. It appears that about a quarter past one oVock the old man, who is rather hard of hearing, WAS in the act of crossing the branch line of railway near the works, when some waggons, which were being run into the works, caught him knocked him on the. metals, and ran over him, breaking both his legs, and other- wise seriously injuring him. The man (Benjamin Anders) who had charge of the waggons, bearing a shout, stopped the train, and on looking round saw the poor old fellow lying' between the metals. Ha was got out of his unpleasant position and taken to the surgery of Dr. Parker, who sub- seqnently ordered him to be removed to the Royal Infirmary at Liverpool. It is a remarkable fact that Robinson, before 1 this accident happened, according to his own statement, has not been laid up for a single dty with sickness of any description Whatever for between 20 and 30 years.

(Rear, hear.) In- stead of .applying themselves to that great question for the benefit of the people, the Government frittered away the time of Parliament in useless talk, and in discussing bills which if they were carried would be pr.ctically of no use. For instance, the time of the House of Commons was occu- pied in discussing whether a man whom ne one would wish to associate with should be admitted into the House of Com- mons, and whom the house had decided it would not admit. Mr. ToccusrowE seconded the motion, which wasadopted, and the proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

THE BOUNDARY QUESTION AT RUNCORN. On Thursday a meeting of the ratepayers of the town- ship of Runcorn, was held in the Commissioners' Board room, for the purpose of considering a public notice issued by the Local Government Board, under the Divided Parishes and Poor Law Amendment Act, 1876, and Poor Lew Act, 1879, with reference to a pro- posed alteration of the boundaries of the townships of Runcorn and Halton. Amongst those present were Messrs. W. Handley, W. Whittaker, Dr. McDougall, Wm. Dyer, Wm. Rushton, John Janion Thos. Riley, Joseph Ormson, Joseph Gleave, Thomas Bowyer, Wm. Brookes, M. Barker, W. Sutton, Thomas Handley, Meadosvcroft, and Bridge- water. Mr. Wm. Handley was voted to the chair; and there was a fair attendance. The proceedings, which it had been expected would have been extremely lively, were of the tamest possitle description. Dr. McDougall may be said to have been the only speaker upon the question, with the ex- ception of the Chairman, and he seemed in capital form for dealing with an opmeent, but not a solitary one opened his mouth. The proposed boundary between Halton and Run- corn suggested by the Runcorn Board of Guardians, is as follows :—"From Halton brook, along Astmore-lane to the bridge thence following Smith's-lane and fences to the river; from Halton brook, down the south side of Wood-lane to its junction with Heath-road, thence up the south side of Heath-road, to the Weston boundary, thence along the present boundary of Runcorn and Weston." The CHAIRMAN said that in 1876 the Govermient passed an Act on purpose to regulate the boundaries of parishes in unions which were very much intermixed. In 1877, there came a communication to, the Runcorn Board of Guardians, asking if there were any townships in the Runcorn Union which were intermixed within the meaning of the Act. Maps were sent up to the Local Government Board, and the Government received such a nnmber from various parts of the country, that they found it necessary to pass another Act. The question, however, remained for some time in , abeyance, because it was found that the townships veered more hopelessly intermixed than was at first supposed. It I was discovered that Runcorn, though not so bad as some places in the country, was quite bad enough; and in 1879, when the new Act became law, the Board of Guardians re- ceived a further communication from the Local Government Board asking for details as to the parishes which were inter- mixed. A committee was formed to draw up a scheme of new bonndaries for such parishes. The committee con- sidered the matter at several meetings, and ultimately drew out a boundary for Frodsham to which, he believed, the ratepayers had consented, at a meeting held recently. Having glanced at the proposed boundary of Runcorn (as given above), he said that if it were carried out, it would have the effect of handing over a large p.oportion of the land which Runcorn had in its district to the township of Halton, in lieu of that to be taken from it. This was the question which they had to consider. If the proposed holm- dary scheme were adopted, Runcorn would hate to maintain the whole of the highway called Heath-road, and only have the rateable value open one side of it with which to do the work. Dr. McDonesALL thought the Chairman had very fairly stated the case in his dual capacity of a poor-law guardian and chairman of that meeting. Difficulties would sooner or later arise if they were to consent to the scheme which the guardians intended to recommend at the Local Government Board inquiry, to be held at Frodsham. There was a certain part of Halton which the Commissioners would na doubt consider it desirable to include in their boundary, but they were asked to take in Halton-road, which was certainly, not great acquisition. It must not be forgotten that the people of Runcorn bad paid burial board rates for 22 years, and it wag scarcely to be ,expected they should confer upon the people in Halton-road privileges to which they certainly werelnot entitled. If the Runcorn people looked at the question from a commercial point of view, it simply meant that if they adepted the suggested boundary, they would be giving to the inhabitants of Halton-road a present of 21 years' rates paid in the township of Runcorn. Then there was the all important msestion of the School Boatel, which, in his opinion, ought to prove an unsurmountable difficqlty in the way of carrying out the suggested boundary, for if it were ratified they might de-1 pend upon it the time would not be long before an additional school was required for Halton-road. They must not forget that the passing of the Canal Boats' Act had probably given them the children of about 800 boat people to provide education for in the future, owing to the number of boats registered in Runcorn. The improvement district should, in fact, be co- ordinate with the pariah. Hitherto the people of the Halton portion of Runcorn had been paying two rates, viz., under the improvement district embraced by the Commissioners and under the rural district. He must tell the meeting that a drainage scheme for the property in Halton- road would probably, cost £4,000, and if the money were borrowed from an insurance company. It would take £2OO a year for '3(f years, to pay tl.e principal and interest, so that the Commissioners would be out of pocket upon the district rate. He proposed a reso- lution to the effect that the meeting disagreed with the pro- posed. boundary in toto, and decided that a deputa- tion, consisting of the Rev. Canon Barely, Messrs. Thomas Riley, James Pritchard, Peter Briscoe, and Dr. McDougall be appointed to wait upon the Local Government Board in- spector at the proposed enquiry at Frodsham in June. Mr. THOMAS RILEY seconded the proposition, which was carried unanimously. In the course of a desultory discussion. it was suggested that Mr. Norman should be appointed a member the depu- tation, but Dr. McDougall reminded the meeting that they must not forget that the gentleman in que.stion was on the side of the opposition in what they were doing. He also said he believed he was correct in stating that the views of Canon Barclay were in accordance With the resolution just passed. Mr. Strrrote, in reply to a question, said the rateable value of the land proposed to be taken from the township of Runcorn and added to Halton and the suggested new boundary, was £3Bl 13s 4d, the rateable value to be taken from Halton £2,347 lOs Bd. The present rateable value of Runcorn was £47,587 16s Bd, and if the proposed boundary were adopted it would be £49,505 14s. The Casual/kw then pointed out on the ordnance map what he and other gentleman considered wculd prove a fair bounder?. He explained that it was one which would add certain detached parts of Runcorn to Halton, and at the Stonehills would continue along Wood-lane; by Halton Grange, to its junction with fleath-roall. The rateable value of these portions would be—Halton, detached, £733 2a.; and ha addition thereto it would take from the town- ship of Halton £312 2s 6d, and £ll2 from the rateable value of Runcorn. ' On the motion of Dr. McDougall, seconded by Mr. John Davies, it was resolved unanimously that the line suggested by Mr. Handley be fail:pitted to the Local Government Board inspector, as the amended boundary. The proceedings then terminated. h

----- SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A. CIULD AT PERSCOT.-011 Thursday afternoon a serious accident happened to a little girl named Elizabeth Goldson, seven years of age, daughter of a labourer named James Goidson, residing at St. Helens- road, Prescot, by which she lost two of he;. fingers. Be- tween three and four o'clock in the afternoon the little girl was climbing up a wall, when she fell, and a large stone weighing about 401 ti. dropped upon her right hind, sever- ing one finger and smashing the other. She was taken to the surgery of Dr. Morris, where it was found necessary to amputate the fingers at the sockets.

ALLEGED ABDUCTION OF A CHILD AT PRESCOI'.—On 'Tuesday considerable excitement and surprise was created in Prescot, in consequence of a little girl named Ellen Wright, six years of age, daughter of Thomas Wright, a . watchmaker, residing in Houghton-street, having suddenly disappeared. It appears that about two o'clock in the ' 'afternoon the child along with an elder sister went out to play, and were subsequently joined by another playmate, and the trio in the course of their rambles get into the Market-place. 'While looking through a draper's shop win- I dow they were accosted by a man who represented himself as their uncle. He asked Wright's girls where their father was, and they replied " tip shop." tie then asked the younger sister, to go with him and he would gather her some flowers, and then take her to her father, at the same time telling the others to wait until they came back. The little girl went with the man, and nothing more was seen or heard of them till about four o'clock when two young women, pro- needing along Shaw-lane, 'Whiston, noticed a young man with a little girl, who was crying most bigerly. As soon as the man saw them he left the child andAn away, but not before the women had recognised him. Fern the statements of the little girl and the women in. questien it would seem, apParently, that the fellow had taken the girl with him for no good purpose. The occurrence was brought under' the , notice of the police by the Nrents of the child, and a thorough investigation into the circumstances is being . made.

THE DIVIDED PARISHES AND POOR LAW AMEND- MENT ACT, 1876, A.ND POOR LAW ACT, 1879. RUNCORN CRIO To the Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester t To the lUventeers of ties Poor, Owner; of Property, and Ratepayers of the Townships of Antrobus, Frodsham, Halton, Norley. Run- eorn, and Seven Oaks, in the said County: To the 'Overseers of the Toor. WHEREAS the Townships of Antrohos, Predsham, Halton, Norky, Runcorn, and Seven Oaks, and the Lord- ship of F. rodsham, in the Runcorn 'Union, in the County of Chester, are divided so that parts of the said Townships and Lordship are isolated and detached from tharemainder, within the meaning of the Divided Parishes and Poor Law Amendment Act, 1816, and the Poor Law Act, 1879; end whereas it has been proposed, in pursuance of the said Act., that each of the said isolated and detached parts be sepamtqd from the said Townships and Lordship, and be amalcamated with sonte Parish or Township which it adjoins, or be otherwise dealt with under the said Acts: and whereas it has teen represented that parts of the Township oPProdsham and the Lordship of Prod- ' sham, although not isolated •acid detached from the remainder of the Township or Lordship, are so situa,ed as to render the relief of the Poor in or the local 'government of, such parts in conjunction with the residue of the Township or Lordship in- convenient, and that it is desirable that the said parts ot the said Township and Lordship should be separated therefrom and be amalgamated with the Township or Lordship in which the same may be locally included, or to which they may be annexed, so that the boundary between the said Township and Lordship shruld "commence at the Helsby Boundary on the north side of the milwarto Smithy-lane, thence up Smithy-lane and the Church footpath to Pinmill-brow, thence up Howey- lane to Overton, thence along Towntield-lane, and down the Occupation-road numbered 307 in the Ordnance Survey, and in the line of tence between 312 and 313, thence along the fence between 312 and 315, and between 275 and 276; all in the Ordnance Survey, to the river. All property lying to-the south of the said boundary to be in the Township of Frodsham Lord- ship, and all property lying to the north of the said •bom Mary to be in the Township of Frodsham ;" or further, that the boun- dary be otherwise altered as may seem to be desirable in pursuanc of the said Acts; and whereas it has also been repre- ssnted that parts of the Townships of Halton andßuneorn, although not isolated.and detached from the remainder of the Townships, are so situate as to render the relief of the Poor in, or the local government of, such parts in conjunction with the residue of the Townships inconvenient, and that it is desirable that the said parts of the said Township; should be separated therefrom. and be amalgamated with the Township in which the ame may be locally included, or to which they may be. • annexed, so that the boundary between the sold Townships should "be from Hilton Brook', along Astmoreslarie to the bridge, thence following Smith's-lane and fences to the tiver ; from Halton Brook down south side of Wood-lane to its junc- tion with Heath-road, thence up the south side of Heath-road to the Weston Boundary, thence slong the present boundary of Runcorn and Weston ;" or further, that the boundary be other- wise filtered as may seem be be desirable io pursuance of the hold e said Acts: and whereas the Local Government Board have qguiivreyn,lnint epfenrermenmto appointed Richard Ingram Dansey, Esquire, Barristerat-Law, souncehopf rtohpoeirsalln:s_peeNtoo, Inspectors, Wig thereforeL°Zrlebi; of the said Acts, that the said Richard Ingram Dansey will attend at the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Thursday, the Second day of• June, 1881, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, to hold a Local Inquiry into the matter aforesaid, when and whereat! persons Interested' in the Subject of the said Inquiry may attend, and state their objections (if any) to an order being made by the Local Government Board in conformity. ,with the provisions of the said Ants. TERRIBLE DEATH NEAR ST. HELENS. _ A PECULIAR TEETOTAL DRINK. An inquest was held on Thursday at St. Helens Junction, by Mr. C. E. Driffield, county coroner, on the body of James Cowan, aged thirty-four, who was found dead on the main line of the London and North-Western Railway, with his skull smashed and arm broken, on Monday morning last. Sergeant Banks represented the police authorities, and Mr. Bash the railway company. John Molloy said that he and deceased worked together as nightsoil-men for the St. Helens Corporation. On Sun- day afternoon he and deceased walked to Liverpool, think- ing to catch the half-past eight train to St. lielens. When they got on the platform the train was just moving off, and they went to the Grapes Hotel, where deceased kad a glass' 11 of sherry wine. I The Coroner : Was not deceased teetotal ? Witness: Yea, sir. They call that teetotal wine. The Coroner: But that is not teetotal stuff. Witness : R is reckoned so, sir. The Coroner: And you are teetotal too? Witness: Yes, sir. I take nothing stronger. The Coroner: Then you were both teetotal. Witness, continuing, said be left deceased and came back by the 'bus to Prescot, deceased intending to return by train later. The Foreman (to witness) said he thought teetotallers did not taste intoxicating drinks. The Coroner: They have their own rules; you had better not interfere with them. George Fletcher, of 16, Albert-road, Edge-hill, guard of the coal train which left Edge-hill at 55 a.m. on .Monday for St. Helens Junction, said they were drawing up to the signals when he saw the body of a man lying about a yard outside the up-line. He dropped off the brake and looked at deceased, who was quite dead. His head was cut and his arm broken. Witness judged that he had been knocked there by a train. Thomas Taylor, of Herbert-street, ticket-collector at St. Helens Junction, said deceased arrived there by the 11-27 passenger train from Liverpool; on Sunday night. Ile ap- peared to be very forward in drink, and sleepy, and had to be helped out of the carriage. When asked for his ticket be fumbled about his pockets, but not being able to find a • ticket was charged one shilling, which he paid and then left the station, through the gate in the proper way. He could not say how deceased had got on to the line again, unless he had got over the goods gate, which was about five feet high, but easy for a sober man to climb. Mr. Bush, the Junction stationmaster, thought deceased had intended to take the line to St. Helens, and bad got down the main lie° towards Liverpool. Although his hat was cut through, and his head badly cut, it was remarkable that not a drop of blood was on the hat The railway ticket and a in money was found in his possession. The Coroner said no doubt the deceased had come to his death accidentally. Ile bad got over the gate and taken the wrong line, going towards Liverpool instead of the line to St. Helens. Mr. Bush said that between the time he was seen and found seven trains would be passing 'on the line. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.
